div.head: LADIES' LETTER.
div.p: LADIES' LETTER.
MY Dzerr. NEusE,

Preparations for the holidays entail the laying aside of much of the elaborate aide of the ward- robe. Four years ago a serge costume could be 'worn all day long, and was changed at dinner- time for a demi-toilette gown. As to jewellery, it never went further than a few rings on the fingers and a pearl necklace. Now, the afternoons bring out a crop of dresses fit for a garden party, and in strong contrast with the serges, linens, and hol- lands worn in the mornings. Diamond brooches Sash from the front of these, and the connection seems almost broken between the seaside and sim- plicity. This is regrettable, for it is an offence against good taste to dress seriously for a stroll on the cliffs or a seat near the band-stand. At dinner, too, the habit of wearing full dress seems creeping in by degrees. An evening blouse used to pass indifferently well at hotel table d'hUte, but now there are required gowns, bodices, square or N-shaped, or half-high, and sleeves of the same sort as are seen in many a full-dress gown, defining the arms to the elbows, and ending there to frill of lace and chiffon.

For very gay o, imag:nable toques of crinoline in pale colours aser in high favour. The shapes ar3 most fanciful, and deftly-pleated and twisted crinoline is mixed with loops and bows of wide, soft satin ribbon. There is rarely any further trimming beyond a spangled .aigrette, or-some cut jet or paste ornaments. The large turban toques-of swathed tulle are also still in fashion, especially in black or white. The latest departure in travelling headgear is a soft ot large Tam o'Shanter cap of cloth or serge to match the travelling dress or cloak. The cap is also nrach affected by those who go in for motor-car trips. Panama hats with just a narrow ribbon round the crown remain in vogue for boating and cycling, and seem to have almost entirely re- placed the long popular sailor shape. Boat-shapes in burnt straw trimmed with scarves of black Limerick lace are in good taste, especially for th. wear of ladies not quite in their first youtu.

Black is one of the worst selections for a travel- ling dress possible, for it shows every speck of dust, and soon gets rusty, besides being hot- looking. Grey, beige, and brown are the best shades, though blue is always popular, being a proved example of gocd-wearing qualities. Barage is a material which is both cool and light to wear, ard being soft, it does not crush easily. When the travelling dress is to combine the mountaineering and walking costume as well, nothing comes up to a stout serge or homespun, neither of which cares abut hard usage nor a wetting. The pretty white-flecked homespuns are the smartest-looking, and as they are invariably made up with a abort coat or bolero, they admit of any blouse which attunes itself to some colouring in the weaving, and a batiste collar, removable at will, tabrighten up the outside. The smartest hats for travelling are th straw or light beaver marquise shapes, which require no trimming but a bow, or a quill in front, with the edges usually bound with velvet. The crumpled straw toque is another useful head- gear, for its fantastic curves and twists supply all the trimming needed, sometimes a quill being thrust through the straw in front.

A good stock of bloirses should be ta.kon, of tile uncrushable kind; a couple of light viyella ones, trimmed with guipure, two or three silk shirts, and a couple of batiste ones ; whilst for dressy occasions a cream satin slip, with speed lace yoke, looks as well as anything. For table d'hote wear a light fculard or &amine costume, covered with lace incrustations, looks nice, but manY people prefer a nice skirt of voile or crepe de Chine, with a handsome blouse, as it admits of more variety. Your loving JE LIMB.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

Nearly a year bas still to elapse before the Coronation of His Majesty, but already the Peers and Peeresses are thinking of their claims and privileges, and their Coro- nation robes and dresses.- The robe to be worn by the King will be woven in this country, in the same design as that worn by Queen Victoria at her Coronation in 1838. There is a strong feeling that all the great ladies who are to be present at the ceremon7 of the Coronation should wear dresses built exclusively of British or Irish made materials and workmanship. The King's robe will be of gold coloured silk, brocaded with the sham- rock, rose, and: thistle, in gold and silver thread, and it is hoped that the Royal example will be generally followed, and thus help to restore British silks and brocades into favour.

The style of the British Sovereign has undergone nstmy changes, but it has only been altered once since George 111. abandoned the title of King of France, just atbundred years ago; and that was in 1816, when Queen Victoria was made Empress of India. It is sow propos- ed to include the Colonies in the Royal title, whirh crou:d tble: read : " Edward VII, by ttrie Grace of Ged, of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland,and of all the British Dominiens beyond the Seas, King, Defender of the Faith, Emperor of India." The addition of the words" British Dominions beyond the Seas " is generally acknowledged to be most appropriate. It was thrugbt that His Majesty might assume the title of " King of all the Britains," after the analogy of the "Czar of all the Russias," but we must clearly abandon all idea of discovering a new word or title, whic:l would include Englishmen, Scotsmen, Australians, and Canadian. in one denomination. Not much has been heard on this side of the vieit of the Dike and Duchess of Cornwall and York to Aus, calla On the whole the visit has been a great success, th, ugh it seems that both the Duke and Duchess failed to make any striking impression on the Colonial mind, and the Duchess appears to have wearied of the perpetual sight seeing and receptions of the past two or three months. Their Royal Highnesses ate now on their way to South Africa, and they will no doubt appreciate the long rest which the voyage will give them. They have yet to visit South Africa and Canada, where there will be plenty to see and do,and it is nearly three months before their return to Portstrouth,where the Duke and Duchess are expected on November 2nd. One of the features of the past season bas been the throwing open of Apsley House. the London residence of the Duke and Duchess of Wellington. It has not the stately proportions of Stafford House, o. Lanidowne House, but it is rich in historic associations with the great Duke, and therefore possesses more than usual interest for the general public. It was here that the Waterloo banquet used to be held, over which the great Duke presided for many years, but his successor, who did not care about living in London, practically kept the place shut up. Now the doors of Apaley House have once more been thrnwn open to Society, and it was the scene of one of the great garden parties of the season, and of other en- tertainments, including the reception by the Duke and and Duchess of Eh,. memb, es of the Briti.h Congress en Tu'

_ iberculosis. The mansion is also open to visitors, on one day of the week,who however should firFt apply for , orders to Colonel Cozen, the private secretary of the Duke of Wellington, at Aps'ey Rouse. Our varied climate greatly adds to the troubles and worries of packing for the holidays, since it is necess- ary to provide for so many kinds of weather. One day it is hot enough for rouelins, thin white serge, or linens and hollands,while the next may be sufficiently cold for the heavy tailor made skirt and coat, and not infre- quently in the evening a winter cape or coat is not no welcome. It is our varied climatic cot dltions that adds so consieeranly to the bulk of our luggage of which the reason thereof Pater familias can never understand. Still in spite cf all grumblings about the size end num ' bee of packages, it is always advisable to provide suffi- ciently against cold and chilly thys. Convenient for the sea-sido woman, are the watez- proof hags, now provided to 114.1 d :he bathing costume. These receptacles take up bet little room to pack(indeed may be en.trusted to take down the family sponges in safety) and on arrival at the watering-place, are in daily requisition. They are not intended to support a great weight, but the gown, towels, comb-bag, novel, tansy work, etc., can all be put into them. These bags are by no means ugly, and are of plain and practical shape, made with a running to bold the draw cord at , the base of a stylishly deep frill. Few things are so , "dowdy " as a bag with a narrow heading. At the seaside, many little people are allowed to run ba•efoot, and this ig really more corn fertable for them than are sandals. Sandals seem to threw all their weight on the great toe, on which devolves the duty of lifting up the foot gear at every step. On clean sands, bare feet give a delicious vn.e of freedom, though even here, there is danger of sharp shells cutting the feet,bUt to go shoelessover pebble beaches and the ordinary inland paths is to run great risk ot wounds, rendered dangerous by added dirt Sand shoes that fit, and boast soft shoo laces, are as sensible as anything,neither locks or stockings are nectssary with them, and they are ready for walking on dry paths, or ieto the edge of the sea. Truly they get water-logged and dirty, but they are almost as easily washed and dried as the little feet which they protect. What to choose at the sales—which still run merrily on—is a problem to be solved only by the wisest. As a rule, finery is never a good investment, the beautiful muslin gowns that aresbeing almost given away just now being a case in point. For immediate wear they are 4elightful, but see not worth putting away. Millinery, parasols, ruftl•-, made-up lace, all mark the elate, and store badly. Really useful bargains are boots and shoes, under- linen, dressing gowns, and tea jackets, and other things, whose fashion changes slowly—good under skirts are likely to come in, as there is plenty of stuff in them, and dresses can scarcely get fuller or longer round the feet. But much depends upon the amateur dress maker, or the clever maid who can adapt and altPrigarna ents quite unwearable in their present form. Fairly large remnants of stuffs, and of ribbons, and of piece and narrow lace, are generally worth seizing upon provided that neither colour nor pattern is so destructive as to mark them as " last year's novelties."

_ A nearer approach to an effective carpet sweeper,than yet introduced, seems likely to be obtained by a new machine using compressed air. This method of clean , ing carpets, when taken up, has long been in use, and the machine which bas not yet been adapted to small rooms, applies the same principle of blowing the dust eutlof the carpet when down, wad collecting all the dirt in a receptacle. This method, if it could be adopted to small and in-expensive household machines, would be a great improvement,as the roller sweepers, so commonly in use, are ve:v wearing to the csrpet, and do not thoroughly take up the dust and dirt. " MADGE "

On Twviday, a middle-aged gentleman,while bathing at Port Skillion, Douglas Head, swam tlo far from shore and was being carried away by a stroag tide. Fortun- ately pleasure yacht No 27 recognised the danrter,and at once put about to the drowning visitor's assistance. Be was picked up much exhausted, thanks to the prompt- ness of John Belly, who was in charge of the yacht.

div.head: EXAMINER, FRIDAY, AUGUST 2, 1901
div.p: THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY, AUGUST 2, 1901

preferred to the companionship of human beings. But, because he was good, I knew that he would come to me without delay, and I was not dis- appointed. I could hardly wait to answer his questions as to my health and spirits when he arrived, but burst at once into the subject weighing on my heart. "Mr. Westerley,4J asked, abruptly, "is it true that—that Lady Cope adopted me when I was a baby—that 1 was not her own child? " The wrinkled old face, with its long, narrow oval, and its high forehead thatched with white hair, flushed deeply, and looked more startled than ever. "Who—who told you this ? " the vicar questioned, with an exaggeration of his usual slight stammer. "Sir Roger Cope," I answered. "He said that you, too, knew the story—only you and he in the world now since my—since Lady Cope is dead. I wouldn't believe it until I had seen you. • But now I know—just from your face, even before you speak—that it's true. "My poor child! It is indeed true. But I had hoped—l knew that Lady Cope had not wished yos ever to be told that you were not her daughter by birth, as you were in heart." We had both been standing up. In my impatience I had not given him the chance of sitting down; but now I sank upon a sofa and covered my face with my hands. The vicar sat beside me, and laid his hand on my head. "Don't take it so hardly, my dear," he said. "She loved you and you loved her. That is the principal thing. I don't know why it was necessary for you to be told, though Sir Roger, no doubt, did what he thought was his duty. But at all events, no one else need know. .Nothing need be changed." "Everything is changed I " I exclaimed. "Because everything that I thought was mine is Roger Cope' s. " Mr. Westerley sprang to his feet with an ejacula- tion of amazement or incredulity. "No I" he said. "No; that cannot be. Lady Cope was too just, too loving a woman, strange as were some of her ideas. She brought you up to consider yourself an heiress—"

"I'm a beggar," I broke in. "She left no will, so Roger says. He was her solicitor, and knew all her business. He told me that he had often advised her to make one, but she put it off. Yet it isn't that I care for I—l've had eighteen happy years. I oughtn't to ask for more. If she bad lived and loved me I wouldn't have minded being poor and leaving dear old Arrish Mall--" . "Surely you—won't be called upon to leave? stammered the vicar.

For an instant I was tempted to tell him the story of Roger's offer and my. refusal of it. But it seemed a dishonourable thing for a girl to do; and instead, I merely explained that, as everything now apparently belonged to Roger, who was, as far as knew, LadySope's only surviving relative, I pre- ferred not to be indebted to him.

_ "There are things I can do to earn my own living," I went on. "I speak French very well; I sing and play; I can paint a little; and, thanks to poor Miss Fitch, my governess, who Was with me for so many years, I have a good all-round educa- tion. I ought to find something to do." "If only I were not a miserable bachelor, my child, you'd not be at a loss for a home," said the kind old man. "Even as it is, I wonder if some- thing couldn't be arranged. it's—it's unbearable to think of you alone in the world. But, thank goodness, it hasn't come to that yet Sir Roger Cope is human. I have always, until now, supposed him a singularly high-minded young man. He will tell you to look upon this house as yours since he can't possibly want it—" "I think he does want it," I cut him short. "And anyway, it would never be home to me again —not for a day It seems, too, that I'm not alone in the world. Roger says my mother is alive and he knows where I can find her. I shall go to her, Mr. Westerley." The vicar's face changed. "I—er—really my child," he faltered, "I should—should do nothing rash if I were you. Better think it over; talk with Sir Roger. Or let me talk with him if you prefer. ies, that is better. I'll see him, and--"
"Thank you, dear Mr. Westerley. He's at the inn, at Lull," I said.

_ A sudden resolution had come to me. There was no use in arguing with this dear old man, who would never either see things as I did, nor make me see them with his eyes. I would let him go now that he had confirmed Roger's statement. And— when I was alone I would make up my mind. "Shall Igo and find Sir Roger now ? " he suggested, with subdued eagerness. I saw, or thought I saw, that he knew some- thing concerning which he feared questions—some- thing which he did not wish to tell. "Yes. It is kind of you," I replied. "Yon have told me that the thing is true, and now—it will be better for me to be alone and think it all over. But is there another mystery, another secret about my real mother ? Why would it be rash ' to go to her ?" "Oh ! " and Mr. Westerley evaded my searching eyes. "You can't tell how she may be situated now, that's all—of course, that's all. There's no mystery. No secret except that which unfor— which Sir Roger has told you. I'll go to him, my dear, I'll go to him. And later I'll come back to tell you the result of our conversation." In spite of his sympathy and kindness he was glad to get away, glad to escape from me. I saw that, and it made me think. But I troubled him with no more questions. If there were a secret I should soon, perhaps, find it out, for I had made up my mind to a very bold step. • Mr. Westerley patted my hand, reassuring me fessily,as best he could; and I bade him good-bye. Yet he suspected nothing. When he had gone I repeated the word with a sob. "Good-bye, dear, sweet old home that I. have loved," I said, with wet, wide eyes that took in every familiar detail of the room. "Good-bye, everything that has been dear. You aren't for me any more. Then the tears which had been held back for so long splashed down. I broke open the envelope which Roger had given me and could scarcely see what he had written. There was more than an address; there was a letter offering me a regular allowance, which I at once resolved to reject. My mother's name I found was Mrs. Newlyn and she lived at 35, Easel-street, Com- mercial-road, Peckham. Having read the letter I wrote a short note to Mr. Westerley, another to Roger Cope. In both of these I said much the same thing, though I said it in very different ways. I told the two men—the old friend of my child- hood, and the cousin who was a cousin no more— that I had decided to leave Arrish Mell at once. Delay would only be painful. I was going to my mother, and would stay with her if she would keep me, though I intended to find work and not be a burden upon her. In any case a letter would reach me if sent to her address. I ended my note to the vicar with grateful, affectionate words; Roger's closed stiffly and abruptly, for I could not make it otherwise, When I had finished,. the hardest part of what I it ad to do was still to come. I had to tell the news to the servants, who had been at Arrish Mell Court for so many years that they had become old friends. It was hard for the loving, simple hearts to understand that I was actually saying good-bye. But they realised it at last; and Evans sorrowfully promised that, when Mr. Westerley and Sir Roger Cope should call after I had gone, he would hand them the notes I had written. There was no time to be lost if I would be away before either the vicar or Sir Roger Cope arrived. In the confusion of my mind at first I had not remembered the present need of money. But sud- denly I flushed and quivered, with• a humiliating thought. "Oh, Swift," I cried, "bring me the green purse • that you put away when—we came back from town.'
CHAPTER VIII. WRAT I FOUND AT THE END OF TILE JOURNEY.

The purse I had desired Swift to bring me was the one which had been in my charge on the night of terror and disaster—the purse that had been rescued for me by a man whose face I had seen once or twice in my dreams since then. On that night it had held a considerable sum, but the money was all or nearly all gone now. There had been frequent calls upon it during the last day or two at the hotel, and though I had supposed then that I should have plenty of my own by-and-bye, I had not cared to apply to Roger while there remained a fund that I could draw upon instead. My hand trembled when Swift gave me the purse. She had been away in the next room longer than necessary it seemed, and I had been desperately ;inpatient to_know my fate. I was almost sure that, at most, there would be left me no more than twenty or thirty shillings,but what was ray surprise when I saw seven bright gold sovereigns. "Oh, lam so thankful " 1 exclaimed. "This will last me a long time." Then, even as I spoke, a torrent of blood rushed up to my face. "Swift, how could you do it ?" I said. "Don't you think I know? Don't you think I understand ? "

"There's nothing to understOnCi, mu,' ehe atturned, stolidly. "I'm sure I can't guess what you mean." "This is your money. You put it into the purse, knowing or" suspecting that I wonld have nothing besides. It was very good, and I thank you; but I can't take it. Tell me how much is yours, Swift, and how much was really there." "Oh, miss, as if I would have dared!" she asseverated. "If there's more in the purse than you expected, why, begging your pardon, it's because of your careless way. You didn't know what you had." "No, but I'm sure----" "Do, do forgive me interrupting, dear miss, broke in Swift. "But it's too bad of you making out I'd have touched your purse—her ladyship': own purse it was, too. It's as much as to say —well, I won't go on, miss, if you look like that. But do tell me you don't believe I would have done it. Now, miss, she hurried on, before I could do more than look what I felt, "I must be hurrying to get ready, too, if you can spare me." "Ready for—what?" I echoed. "Why, to go with you, to be sure." "I thought you understood," I said, sadly, "I can't take you. I must go alone." She burst out crying. "Oh, miss, that's the last straw I must go with you. 'Twoukl be wicked to stand by and let you go out in the world alone—just like a little white lamb in its ignorance straying into the butcher's hands." "I am going to—my mother," I answered, choking a little. "She—isn't very rich, and—and I fancy she must live in a small house. She would not know what to do with a maid, and—besides, I couldn't pay you." "I wouldn't want a penny, miss, and I'd be a 'general,' sooner than leave you," persisted Swift, almost fiercely. I didn't know what she meant by a `general,.' associating that name only with high officers of the army, but I appreciated her intention. We were miserable together; and when I went down to the carriage, there were all the others in the hall, not a dry eye among them. Somehow, I got through the good-byes, and took one last, long, yearning look at the old house as I and my luggage were driven away. I left Lull at two o'clock in the afternoon, Three hours later I arrived at Waterloo Station. My thoughts had been so busy that the journey had not seemed long. Indeed, I had almost dreaded the end, because of the necessity for action it would entail; and besides, I had begun half to repent my rashness in flinging myself upon the world before I was absolutely certain that I could have my mother's protection. When she had been at a distance, I had looked upon her as a sure refuge. Roger had given me her address, and had said positively that she was to be found there. I was her daughter, and it had seemed natural that when the floods of disaster had swept me off my feet, I should try to grasp her hand. Easel-street, Commercial-road, meant nothing definite to me. I vaguely thought of Peckham as a suburb, and I had some dim picture in my mind of a neat little ivy-draped brick house in a small garden, such as I had often seen in the village of Lull. The London I had known best was the segion of parks, big splendid houses, and smart shops. I was not foolish enough to suppose that my mother. who had been described as poor, had her home in such a neighbourhood as that, but, as I was driven through street after street, even meaner and more squalid than the ones I had seen on the night I followed Lady Cope from the Lyceum Theatre, I grew sad and amazed. Was it possible that, while all my life I had lived among beautiful things, the woman who had brought me into the world harl been—here ? At last we turned into a narrow street, lined On either side with little grey houses, all exactly alike. It was as if a wall of dirty brick stretched along, with low doors and windows cut into it at intervals; for there was no separation between the houses. Each hovel had a door of its own, with a window on the ground-floor; and above, two more windows. On the broken pavement, or in the gutters, ragged children swarmed; dwarfish girls carrying big-headed, squalling babies almost as large as themselves; toddling boys, with red- rimmed eyes and grimy faces. The babies all seemed to be crying ; their young nurses shrilly bidding them be still, or exhorting the boys who shouted over their games to come home at once if they did not wish various horrible consequences to befall them.

It was a dreadful street; the worst 1 had ever seen, and I wished that my driver would make has* in passing through. But, to my surprised alarm, he stopped, drawing up the cab at the pave- ment. "He is going to inquire the way," I thought. Yet no; he was clambering slowly off the box. I looked out. We were exactly in front of a door cut in the long grey wall a' blackened brick. Over the door was a number-- 35. My heart gave a leap, and I almost called out a protest. It could not be true. Any place but this, The driver opened the cab door. "Here yos are, miss ; 35, Easel-street," he said, seeing thr... eat still. "Oh, it can't be the right Easel-street!" I exclaimed, tremulously. "Easel-street, Commercial-road. There ain't no other of the same name, miss. Shall I knock ?" _

"If you please," I meekly answered. "And— antl don't take down the luggage yet. I'll wait and see if—if—" My voice died. I did not finish the sentence. There was no bell on the door, which stood ajar. The cabman knocked loudly. From the two upper windows the frowsy heads of several children and a bold-looking young woman appeared. They stared with open-mouthed curiosity at me and the four smart new boxes heaped on the four-wheeler. I shrank back, and wound my fingers nervously together. "What d'you want ? " shrilly demanded the woman. "Miggits or Newlyn ? " I drew my breath in sharply. My mother's name! There was no mistake, then. The cabman turned questioningly to me, and I realised that I must answer. "I want Mrs. Newlyn," I reluc- tantly thrust out my head to explain. "Owh!" returned the dweller on the upper floor, , "I'm Miggits. Newlyn's the ground-floor." As my informant partially withdrew, a girt-- face chewed itself in the crack of the door; the* the door was thrown wide open. She was shot* fifteen, with pale unwholesome skin, a pert nose. and an aggressive fringe of drab-coloured • hoist She fixed a pair of light blue eyes upon me, and slowly I descended from the cab, which seemed the only link left between me and familiar decencies of civilisation. "Is Mrs: Newlyn at home ? " I inquired, in a voice which did not sound like mine, so dull and toneless was it.

"Yes, ma's 'ome." (I started.) "D'ye want to see 'or?" • "If you please. May I—may I walk in ? " Already half the swarming population of Easel- street had come to its doors and windows to enjoy the sight—such as it was. • I felt curiously giddy. The suggestion in one of the first three words this girl had spoken had caught me by the throat. I entered the narrow passage, having again bidden the the cabman wait; and the close odour of the house added to my faintness. A door a few feet down the passage was opened, and I had a dim impression that my com- panion as bidding me follow her into a room beyond. I obeyed, and then almost recoiled as I passed the threshold. The room could not have been more than twelve feet square. The boards of the floor were uncovered, and not too clean; the low ceiling was blackener' with smoke, and the wall, destitute of paper, was decorated with a few glaring, unframed chromo- lithographs, held in place with pins. In one corner was a tumbled bed, covers pillows and all, with a dark calico quilt. Thirt: was one unclothed deal table, spread with a few common dishes and a tin or two; there were three or four rough wooden chairs; a big box, heaped with a strange medley of cooking utensils and women's outdoor wraps; a mantelshelf, littered with odds and ends; and a kitchen range, into which a woman, with her back turned to me, we. throwing 3 few coals from a battered shovel.

"Ma,' 'ere's a lydy—to -see,—;;;,;-.l;usquely announced my guide. The woman turned, shovel in hand. My eyes sought her face wistfully, imploringly, for the one gleam of hope left. But the last flicker died as our eyes met. No subtle voice of nature cried out in my heart: "This is your mother; you are of one flesh and bloOd.“ She was it tall, thin woman who might once have been pretty, even ladylike-looking in better days, but there was hardly a vestige of past beauty remaining, though in years she was not really old. Her scanty, grizzled hair was pulled carelessly back from a lined forehead. Her small mouth had a fretful drop; slightly open, in surprise at sight of the visitor, it shewed that one front tooth was gone. The cheeks were hollowed in, the well- cut nose sharpened, the complexion of the uniform, faded grey most fashionable in Easel-street among those who were not over-florid. She wore a rusty black dress, and a coloured cotton handkerchief was tied round the thin throat instead of a collar.

My tongue clove to thq roof of my mouth. Ilk seemed physically impolssible to tell her who I was, to ask her if she were not my mother. But they were both waiting for my explanations. I had to speak. "I —I hope—' A few lame words had come stammeringly, when the elder of the two broke in. "If you're one of those district visitors, why, I can just tell you as I told the last one, that you ain't wanted here," she said, acidly, with a rather better accent than the girl's. "I —my name is Cope," I stammered. "At least, I always thought it was until to-day." Still she stared at me, with little, if any, awakening comprehension in !lei eyes. I blundered desperately on. "Perhaps, if you don't know what I mean it may be a mistake after all. But Lady Cope is dead. I was brought up to believe her my mother, and now--"
Suddenly the woman's pale face changed and reddened with a vivid flush. The small fire-shovel she had been grasping slid out of her hand and fell to the floor with a metallic crash.

"My goodness, gracious me!" she ejaculated, with a gasp. "It's Jenny." A faint shiver ran through me. I was not even "Sheila" any more. I was "Jenny." "I heard to-day that—that--" I faltered. I could not go on. But she took up the words with a shy, awkward sort of eagerness, as if she were half-afraid of me; while the girl stood by, wide-eyed and dumb in bewilderment. "Did they tell you the whole story? Did they tell you who I was, and all ? " "Sir Roger Cope told me that you were—my mother," I said, dully. "Well, I never He told you that! And after Lady Cope making me swear I'd never breathe a word to a soul so long as I lived." "Oh, ma, it ain't true, is it?" cried the girl. "She ain't my sister? "Hold your tongue and mind your own business," was the sharp answer; and I felt, rather than saw, the flounce of her poor skirts and the toss of her toweled head that the girl gave. The woman looked keenly at me, her face still flushed and excited, half-suspicious; but she did not take a step nearer. "I doN't think Lady Cope meant me to be told," I answerdd, choking back a sob. "But Roger knew from the first. Moth—Lady Cope only died a few days ago, though it seems a long, long time.' "You heard to-day, and you came straight here to see me," said my , newly-found mother, reflectively. "Well, that was very good of you, my dear, that it was. I ,only wish I had a better house for you to come to. But I haven't had any luck. Totsey, get the ydung lady a chair. Dear me, I wonder now if you'd let me make you a cup o' tea ?"

_ She still spoke to me as to a stranger of another class from hers; a visitor who must be entertained. She was nervous, and suddenly she became a pathetic figure in my eyes, though I had no stirrings of love. Perhaps this was unnatural, hard-hearted. I cannot help that, for I must paint the picture truly. I could have screamed or broken into hysterics as Totsey rather sullenly placed a chair for me; but I almost fell into it.

"Is—is it possible that this is my sister?" I forced myself to ask. • "Your half-sister," was the quick reply, as if there were relief,in responding to definite ques- tions. "After Lady Cope adopted you—ft was hard enough to part with my only one, I can tell you, my dear, but what was I to do ?—after she took you away I married again. 'Twas the only thing to do, for 1 wasn't the sort of woman to be left alone. I had two girls by my second husband, a very different sort of man from your father. I thought, though he was but a rough fellow com- pared to him, he'd be a protector. But 'twasn't long before I found out it was the money he was after—the money Lady Cope gave me when she took you." So I had been sold for a price! was the thought that darted through my mind. But I was silent, listening. As she went on there was a loud noise in the passage outside the door. The handle turned. I started and turned round. What was to come now?
(To be continued.)

div.head: GIRL OF THE PEOPLE.
div.p: A GIRL OF THE PEOPLE.
By MRS. C. N. WILLIAMSCN„ Author of "The Earn S'orners," ,"Fortune's Sport," "Miss Nobody," "Her Royal High- ness," "Lady Mary of the Dark House," &a

SUMMARY OF PRECEDING CHAPTERS: Sheila Cope is taken by her mother to the theatre, and there sees two people who interest her strangely. One is a young man in the pit, to whom she is indefintbly drawn, and the other a woman in the stalls. The latter catches Sheila's eye and deliberately exposes a purple scar on her arm. Sheila is startle for 4, similar scar on her mother's arm has teen mystery to her since childhood. When Lady Cope notices the woman with the scar sho hastily leavels the theatre, putting Sheila into a c, ') aid bidding her drive back to the hotel. On her • -ay borne, the girl catches a glimpse of her _mother :d the woman with the scar seated in four-wheeler. Subsequently the young man of the Lyceum pit renders her an important service: When Sheila reaches the hank her mother is not there, but presently arrives in if dying condition, with her right arm horribly scarlet* and a fresh burn where the scar had been. Murmuring incoherently of "the scar—after all these years—revenge," and ',the West Wing," Lady Cope dies of heart disease. It is noticed that she was wearing a black opera-clonk instead of the yellow one in which she went out. Sheila instinctively connects this with the woman of the scar. Next day Sheila. goes down to Arrieh Mell Court, her Dorsetshire home, where her mother is buried. She resolves to carry out her mother's dying wish and investigate the West Wing. After a patient search, during which sheis startled by mysterious noises, she finds nothing but a tiny key in the pocket of an old tea-gown of her mother's. Next day Sir Roger Cope, her cousin, who ignores his title and works as a solicitor, calls. He proposes to her, i and when refused, tells her that she s not the ' daughter of Lady Cope at all, and, as the dead woman left no will, the property belongs to himself as next-of-kin.

div.head: CHAPTER VII.
div.p: CHAPTER VII.
I ARRIVE AT A MOMENTOUS DECISI

"I can understand well enough," I exclaimed, bitterly, "why you should have wished to marry me if I had been the heiress that people hays thought me. But why do you want me now?" Roger waved his hand towards a great mirror that went from floor to ceiling, on the wall of air "Indian boudoir."

"Look at yourself," he said. Mechanically, hardly knowing what I did, I looked. Never before had I been critical of myself. But now I gazed searchingly at my own face—the one fortune that was left me. I was beautiful. Even I could see that. As I grew older, my hair might change its young gold for autumn brown; but it was yellow as ripe wheat now, brown only in the shadows, where the waves curved inward. And my eyes were big, and dark, and soft. Suddenly, I felt very sorry for myself, because I was so pretty, and only eighteen; because I seemed to have left youth and happiness for ever,behind me, and there was no one whom I . loved or had a claim upon to put kind arms round me, and let me cry my heart out on a sympathetic F breast. Tears sprang to my eyes, but I crushed them back. Roger Cope should not see me cry. "I want you because you are the prettiest girl, and some day will be the most beautiful woman, on earth," cried Roger, speaking more warmly and impulsively than I had ever heard him speak, 9 want you, too, because you are hard to win; and I have always liked overcoming difficulties. Sooner or later, I warn you, Sheila, I will overcome this one, and you.with it. I will! You might as well yield to the inevitable now." "It isn't inevitable. And I won't yield," .I stoutly maintained. "You haven't proved any of your statements yet." "I will, soon enough; or, rather, I can. Bat if you will promise to marry, me, sweet, no ono need ever know. You will Marry as Miss Sheila • Cope, of Arrish Mell Court; and I will come hers to live, as your husband—" "You will come here to live, it may be, but not as my husband," I cut him short. "I shall hays gone away before that." "Where would you go? " Roger asked, curiously, almost incredulously. "The world's a big place," I retorted, my voice quivering with the sobs that would not quite be kept back. One tore its way up from my heart; and, with two great tears running down my cheeks, I exclaimed :,"Oh, if there -were only somebody whom I belonged to!" Roger. took a etep forward, and put out his hand, but I pushed it from.me ; and his blue eyeg Bashed their resentment. "I believe," he said, -quietly; in the drawl which had so often stung me to impatience, "that there are several persons with whom you are entitled to claim kinship, if you choose." I dashed my, _tears away, and gazed 'at him eagerly. "Tell me—tell me I " I cried. "How was it that my moth—that Tiady Cope took me as her own child 3 . "She was very unhappy at the time. Five years before she had lost her little son, whom she and her husband both adored. He died in most tragic Circumstances, which changed his mother's whole nature. Sir Vincent and Aunt Ermyntrude we abroad. There Sir Vincent area also, and poor Aunt Ermyntrude came back—not to her old home, but to London. She undertook various charitable works, and it was while she was giving up her life to the interests of others that she met your mother." "My mother!" I echoed, in a whisper. For a moment I was powerless to ask more; but Roger went on, without waiting for my questions. "Your mother was also a widow, and very poor. You were her only child, but she had been ill, among other misfortunes, and was hardly able to provide for you. Aunt Ermyntrude saw you—a pretty little thing a few months of age; and, taking a great fancy to you, in her loneliness, offered to adopt you as her own. Your mother finally con- sented, and as Aunt Errnyntrude had been living abroad for several years with her husband, and her presence in London had been known to none, nobody was particularly surprised when she came home at last with a baby not quite a year old. "I knew the truth from the first, because I had visited Cousin Vincent and Aunt Ermyntrude abroad, and knew that they had no child, so I had -to be told. And the vicar, old Mr. Westerley, was told also, but we were both asked to keep the secret, and we always have._"
"You said that'some of my people were still alive," I said, in. a.strained voice.

"Your mother is living," Roger quietly answered. "I have been at some pains to keep track of her —for Aunt Ermyntrude's sake, of course." Somehow I did not believe that it had been for anyone's sake but his own, and for some purposo which I seemed to be on the point of discovering. "I have your mother's present address. if you wish to write her, Sheila," Roger said. "Shall I give it to you ? " "Yes," I said, "I want the address. But, before writing, I should like to see Mr. Westerley. You told me that—he knew the secret also."

"He does," Roger answered, gravely. "And you shall see him. I understand what is in your mind. You believe that I am deceiving you. Well, it is natural, perhaps—though it's hard to be misjudged by the woman" one loves. In the mouths of two witnesses, it is said, a truth shall be established; and the sooner you hear what Mr. Westerley can add to my statement, the better I shall be pleased. Not—l wouldn't have you think that for a moment I—not that I'm not only too glad to have you stay here as long as you will, even if we are to be nothing to each other." "I will send a carriage down to Lull, and ask Mr. Westerley to come out at once," I cried ; then bit my lip. The carriages were Roger's. But I let it pass. Until I was sure, I would grant myself some privileges, with the benefit of the doubt. Roger rang the bell, and then came back to me. From his pocket he took • sealed envelope. "The address you wanted," he explained. "I will go_ and leave you alone now. I can see that you would prefer that. After Mr. Westerley has been with you, and gone away again, you shall have a little time to think. Then I will me back, and you shall tell me what decision have reached. It 04 may be that you will look Upon matters with a different eye. At all mitts, remember that while you have me, you are not friendless." He held out his hand, and though I felt the impulse to refuse it, I would not, lest he should think it was because I grudged him the things that Ind seemed mine. When the bell was answered, a servant was informed that the carriage I ordered might take Sir Roger Cope back to the inn before calling for Mr. Westerley. The vicar was a kind old man with a nervous I manner, and the air of being slightly startled when 1 anyone addressed him. His greatest pleasure was collecting butterflies. a pastime which he infinitely

div.head: WATER POLO. --- Liverpool and District League.
div.p: WATER POLO. --- Liverpool and District League.
Everton Defeat Warrington.

The space allotted to spectators at —the Warrington ' Corporation Baths was compietely filled on Tuesday ivenine, when an enthusiastic audience assembled to witness the league polo match between Warrington and Everton. The Liverpool team has the reputation of• being one of the best in the district and their visits to Warrington always arouse much interest. On Tuesday evening the visiting team arrived an hour late, baying iMrsed their train at Liverpool. Mr McDonald of Liver-, poi was the referee, and the teams entered the bath as ' follows :—Everton, Morris, goal ; A Newcombe and J Gosnersal, backs ; D Nevin' half back ; C Formby, J Formby, and T Towers, forwards. Warrington, A Rote rtson goal ; A Boscow, A Ashton, backs ; W Ashton 'fait back; J Hughes, C Ashton aud J Sutton, forwards. During the first half Warrington defended the deep end, and at the outset Everton attacked Nog, rously. Several shots were aimed at the ' Warrington goal, but for a time Robertson was equal to ail emergencies. Eventually, however, J Formby proved, so to speak, one too many for kim, and regis- tered the first goal for Everton. Or resuming, play was immediately carried into the borne team'a territory, and C Formby scored. Warrington now played up more tiriskly, and Ashton sent in a good shot, but Morris ved. Half-time arrived with the score: Everton, two tolls ; Warrington, nil. After the interval play was of an:even character, both'goals:being frequently assailed. Kaborton was several times applauded for his neat work t the home goal. Eventually Boscow obtained posses- sion and threw the whole length of the bath to Hughes, ho dribbled past Morris and scored. The game now became quite exciting and C Ashton and Towers had to. b cautioned for rough play. There was no furtner scoring, Everton being the victors by two goals to one.

div.head: SOME CARNEGIE METHODS.
div.p: SOME CARNEGIE METHODS.

-- The Pitt.,burg Bessemer and Lake Erie Railway. owned by the Steel Company, Is a new road build ea- tlusiVely for the ore and coal trade. There are used ome of the heaviest engines ever built, hauling a lone , rain of immense steel gondola hopper cars holding 50 tons of ore apiece. This road forms a direct line from Conneaut to Pittsburg. When these ore trains reach the Carnegie furnaces they must be unloaded as quickly as possible, to save cars and to save storage track toom The cars are stopped on the platform of a tipple and clamped down to the track. The tippet is then tet in metion, lifting a section of the track, aded car and all, and turning it through a v ertical circle until the car is turned upside down and the 50 tons more or less, of ore are emptied into bucket cars, wh.ch stand on a track alongside. This machine is guaranteed to handle 300 cars in a day of 10 hours. These bucket cars are hauled away to the side of the stock yard and stopped under the cantilever of the largest bridge tramway ever built. This tram- way has a trolley travel of about 500 feet, and can pick up the bucket with its load of 22,100 pounds from the car, and carry it to any part of the yards. This load of over 10 tons can be lifted from the ground at the rat, of 210 feet per minute, can be moved across the bridge at a speed of 800 to 900 feet per minute, and the whole machine, load and all, can be moved up or down the ,ards at a speed of 75 to 100 feet per minute.—The " Engineering Magazine."

div.head: HOME AGAIN.
div.p: HOME AGAIN.

Warrington Volunteers Return fronl Salisbury Plain. After having undergone a fortnight's coarse cf training at Perham Down, Salisbury Plain, tile Warrington Volunteer Battalion retuned home •I! Saturday evening. They arrived in three special trains, and a large number of townspeople baa assembled to witness their home coming. 1116 battalion paraded in the morning at half-past seta the first train starting at half-past eight, the secend and third following at intervals of half-an-hour. Is was thought that the Volunteers would arrive after six o'clock, but considerable surprise was ices' sioned when the first detachment were seen walk- ing up Horsemarket-strset at a quarter past five. It consisted of the Mountry Infantry, Cyclist Cora: panies and G Company under the direction 01 Colonel Ridgway, Major Buckton, Captain Gros' field, and Lieutenant Avery—in all about 150. Tin second detachment arrived before six o'clock, an,' was composed of nine companies, whilst five coal; panics, with band and baggage, formed the third train load. As each contingent marched to Drill Hall the route was lined with spectators, the men were loudly cheered. Before they I dismissed, Colonel Ridgway briefly addressed t, with regard to their behaviour in camp which, said, had been exceedingly good. The Brigadi General had spoken very nighly of them, especie the steadiness of all ranks whilst on parade. AL Roome, who is acting as Brigadier-Major to Mersey Brigade, is still under canvas at Peri Down.

High Praise for the Brigadier General. The following brigade orders have, been issued Brigadier-General the Hon Sir Frederick W Scopfi K.C.M.G., C. 8., commanding at Perham Down Cal 26th July,l9ol :—The brigadiPr wishes to convey to battalions forming the 30th Volunteer Infantry Brig his appreciation of the zealous manner in whic' ranks have worked during the fortnight they have in camp. What struck him most was the great h ness displayed by everyone to make the most of opportunities afforded at Salisbury Plain for instruct in practical training in field duties, and, considering few opportunities the battalions have had prioi arrival in camp of working on ground suitable maneuvres, ho thinks that the manner in which training was carried out was most credits to all concerned. The fire discipline was espech satiafactory. The officers, non-commissioned of& and men will have found out the points in which i need further practice, and the brigadier trusts he succeeded in his wish to impress upon them Of traininefor war, individual intelligent appreciath the ground is essential, and that cut and dried fai attack and defence are out of place. He unders, that at the headquarters of the battalions suitalc," ground for field trainhag is limited, but he thinks OW' even in such circumstances good work can be done DV careful study of ground, with a view of seeing how ii would be beet utilised, if available, for attack, defence; outposts' /co. As was to be expected, the behaviour the Men has been excellent. The brigadier hopes Oa' the fortnight's work has been as interesting and instr°c. tive to all ranks as it has been to him and he trust!. that be will again be assoeiated with the 30th Volunteer Infantry Brigade.

The Secretary of the Local Government Board for warded a circular stating that the attention of that boll had been drawn to the many advantages that ba rrsulted from the use of training ships for the instrue; tion and maintenance of boys,and to the advisability Boards of Guardians utilising to an increased extent Olt' means of training for the boys under their care. were fired than Mr Yarwood who heard them P—Yes, about 150 yards. Had you heard any shots from a revolver or from any firearm on that Bunday ?—No. Did you go to Hepplestone, the guasmith's, after the murdek P—Yes. In relation to a revolver which was in your ownership on the 7th of April P—Yes. Did you ask him as to whether he could determine whether a revolver had been fired or not recently ? Yes, that is what I asked him. Did he tell you how to determioe thatil—Not exsotlY ; I wanted him to go with me to Altriocham police- station. That was what I wanted Bepplestone for. Mr Bankes : Were you anxious that any enquiry that could be made should be made P —Certainly, I was. SERGEANT PIERCE'S STORY. Police-sergeant Pierce, will has had the conduct of the case throughout, spoke of his hearing of the murder and to his detaining Parrott. Bould, when he was found murdered, had no money upon him, and his pocket was turned inside out. Sergeant Pierce told the Court that Parrott said he had been to Liverpool on the day of the murder, and had walked from Manchester to Kautsford, which was a distance of 17 miles. _ _
Before charging prisoner with the wilful muder of B )uld witness cautioned Parrott. The prisoaer's reply to the charge was" You are on the wrong track I did not do it."

Sergeant Pierce next came to where the prisoner contradicted his earlier statement, and admitted having worn an overcoat, and having been in Mere Heath-lane. He said that he bought thB revolver for about £4 from Colts, and he had it addressed to 335, Portland-street, Manchester. He had since sold it to a sailor at Liverpool for 50s, and he promised to bring him some smuggled tobacco. The officer described his search of the prisoner's home, and the discovery of the revolver case and the purse containing the farthing and the half-farthing.

div.head: SATURDAY'S PROCEEDINGSNOT GUILTY.
div.p: SATURDAY'S PROCEEDINGS- NOT GUILTY.
EVIDENCE OF THE PRISONER.

I Saturday's hearing was noteworthy from th'r) fact that the defending counsel hastened to take advantage af the rule of criminal procedure which allows him to put I the accused person in the witness box, there to tell his , own story and stand or fall by the cross-examination upon it. Mr Griffith, M.P., whose defence of Parrott was noteworthy for its clearness and determination,had announced on Friday that he would adopt this course, and the promise doubtless bad much to do with the increased attendance of the general public, whose num. hers were augmented as the day wore on. The solicitor's clerk who ferreted out the -shop in Liyerpoci where the .Jubilee counters, one of which was found in Parrott's purse., were sold finished off ilia evid- ence, and then for over a couple of hours-Parrott him- self was under examination. A sparely built, pale com- plexioned youth,with more than a tinge of tedin his hair Parrott had little enough of the criminal look about him as he Stepped into the witness-box. Ile was cool , enough, too. As be sat in the dock he gave-the impres- sion of complete confidence:;' in the witness-box his I answers were ready, and, to the opposing ;Counsel, sometimes a trifle curt. HIS WANDERINGS. . _

His story was to the effect that he spent the Satur- day before Easter Sunday with his brother at Liverpool, and on Sunday morning about ten o'clock he came to Manchester- A little later he started to walk to %nuts- ford, a distance of 16 or 17 miles, and, walking home. he took a choice of coming along the Manchester-road and the Mere Heath-lane, which run nearly parallel, by Choosing the latter. He sat on a gate, and wiped his brow with a handkerchief. Then be went behind a hay- StaCk, but finding that he was visible from the road 4 he crossed the road, entered another field, and went to- wards another shed. As he approached the shed a man came out,asked what he wanted,and told him to" clear out." So he walked back to Mere Eleath-lane,and as he I was entering another gate Miss Francis went by. He also saw two persons—a man and a woman. When he reached linutsford he went down Tatton- street. Be sailed in at the station to meet a train, but it had gone out. Be then went down Adam's Hill to the Leigh Arms,usually known as the Sword and Serpent Inn. He bad a drink there and be was served by Miss Flora Lee. After remaining in the house about ten minutes he went home, had supper, and retired to bed. UNDER CRON EXAMINATION. For nearly two hours the crom-examination of Parrott by Mr Abel Thomas proceededia Counsel first elicited that prisoner still had hopes of going out to West Africa, and then went on to talk about the revolvzr. Parrott took the weapon to aydock Park races with him, and again to Manchester and Liverpool on the 22nd March. What, asked counsel, were you doing with • revolver in your pocket—you were not going to West Africa ? I might have done, all the same. I intended to stay in Liverpool. What was your object in taking your revolver and your cartridges ?—I have already answered you. THE MrSILIERIPIIB BAILOR.

Then came the meeting in Liverpool with the mys- terious sailor to whom the revolver was sold. Parrott did not know his name, nor the ship he belonged to, but he wanted Parrott to apply for a position as cook. They were having a drink together when he showed the sailor the revolver, and the sailor agreed to buy the weapon for a sovereign, and 10s worth of smuggled tobacco, which was to be delivered to him by the sailor at an ion in Orford-street, Manchester, on Friday, March 20th. Mr. Thomas: Having paid £4 15s for the revolver and the case three days before, you sell it for £1 and 101. worth of tobacco. Do you really mean that 2—Yes, I do. Next Mr. Thomas trought prisoner to talk about the events of Easter Sunday. Parrott said that although he had several shillings with him be preferred to walk to Knutsford from Manchester, because there was no train until the afternoon. He first heard of the murder on the following morning. Why didn't you go fta the police. then P—Because I was out of the lane. I was near the station shortly after a quarter to seven, therefore I did not see any horsemen. You were there between six and seven. Why didn't you go to the police P—l had no reason. Did you tell anybody that you were there between six and seven o'clock ?—I have answered you before. Parrott proceeded that Miss Francis, at the inquest. said she saw s man with spectacles, and he did not wish to be mirsed up in the case. Mr Thomas You wanted, I suppose, to find out who murdered —cruelly murdered—f3ould ? Prisoner : Hasid( s, look here, Miss Francis passed rite at the gate, as I came to Knutsford, and I did not see any horsemen. According to the evidence of Parkes,the deceased came down the lane with the horsemen, there. fore I did not see the horsemen, and I was not in the lane. Did you argue that in your mind ?-110, I did not argue. It is clear enough. I want to Itsow your reason why you did not go to the police and tell them all you knew?—Well, there are other people who have not come forward. You say you did not want to be mixed up with the matte ?—i did not wish to be a witness in the ease

div.head: KNUTSFORD TRAGEDY.
div.p: THE KNUTSFORD TRAGEDY.
Tri
Lt Chester Assizes.
Prisoner Acquitted. ,

•On before - rids morning, at Chester Assizes, the trial began -.ore , justice Grantham, of James Crossley Parrott, aged twenty-one, a labourer, charged with the murder Of John Bould, a tailor, in Mere Heath-lane,Altrincham, cal Easter Sunday, April 7th. The prosecution was conducted by M• Abel Thomas, C, M P, and Mr Ralph Bankos, while the prisoner was defended by Mr Ellis Jones Griffith, MP. with whom Wall Mr Lance Bentley' ,The prisoner, a well-dressed, harmless-looking youth, Pleaded not guilty to the charge. Mr Abel Thomas opened the case for the prosecution, ;:,rdetailed the facts of the case which have already en made public. THE EVIDENCE. Thompson Flood, house joiner at Tatton Hall, said that at a quarter past air on the evening in question be aII Proceeding along Mere Heath-lane with his wife 4:lu some children, when be saw • handkerchief being ared behind the hedge. He afterwards saw a man, Whom he identified as the prisoner, crossing a fieid,and t`terwards he saw him en the road with a handkerchief °Mut his hand. He was wearing a dark topcoat, three ;Platter size, similar to the one produced. In til cross- litriination, witness said be had not previously known Prisoner. He was walking in the field quite openly, e luarY Flood, wife of last witness, gave similar aldence. t Dorothy Jackson, a beautifully-dressed little girl, ft'n,elVn years old, said that she was going home to Routs- on the evening in question with Mr and Mrs Flood. 411° eaw the prisoner. wnom she had known by sight, in lane, and she noticed that he had a handkerchief leted round his thumb. le,gthn Parks, gardener at Tatton Park, deposed that be fes Walking along the lane with a young woman on: a e evening in question, when he saw a man fitting on *gate waving a handkerchief: He afterwards saw ~.,orn he believed to be the same one going over another r,o into afield. He also saw the deceased, John Bould, Walking in the direction of Knutsford. attempt n-etsoacmoinnceeda,l witness himself.s aid that the man did not FRANCIS.

Mary j EVIDENCE OF MISS - ane Francis, a waitress at Mrs Speakman's, Knutsord, said that about a quarter to seven she took a walk in the lane. At a gate near some haystacks she !Isar a man whom she identified as the prisoner, but w_ hem she did not know at the time. Lower down the road three horsemen passed her. Two of them stopped, Ibud one dismounting, took hold of her by the waist. Be fad Ike bridle over his arm, and she told him she was fr„!ffhtened of horses. He then gave the horse to his t'l,ehd Yarwood, and he kissed her rather roughly and sled to take liberties with tier She resisted in evert, 71,4,,79 and screamed twice as bard as she could. Rowe ;t4sti let her go, and the two men rode off. During the egle witness heard some shots fired. While walk- a"g hack to Knutaford, she came to a curve in the road, .rscl when she had passed the curve she saw a man lying .41 the hedge, with another leaning over him and doing rtaf thing with his hand over laird. The man who was g'Tng over had on an overcoat, which she took to be grey in colour, and which was •so long that it most tripped him as he went along. iYhen you got round the curve what did be do -P—He "t and went away. I don't know whether he saw roe or not. Was he walking:or running?—Running as hard as life Would take him. „ Proceeding, witness said that while she was hesita c`lq what to do, two men, named Toft and Daniels, ikiwe IV. and it was round, that the man lying on the ground was John Botild, and that he was dead. ,b_W the man who ran away the same as the man you ii Ws, clseeen before ?—I can't swear. What was the impression on your mind at the time ?: do believe it was the same mail in a sense. Cross-examined by Mr Ellis Griffith, she said that she told the coroner that the man had a dark coat, and the other a grey or dark grey coat. She had also said that she eould not say that either the two men or the two coats were alike. Questioned in regard to the assault upon her, she said that Rowe's behaviour lasted about ten minutes. When she screamed the man let her go. You did not scream for ten onion:ea P—No. I had not the strength to scream for ten minutes; but I had Providence given to me when I was in the arms of quite 4, stranger. The police had been to see her many times, she had not spoken about the case to anyone else- olnee the murder she had been staying at Welshpool. Hugh Daniels, gardener. of King-street. Koutsford, !Atated that between 6.30 and seven o'clock on the even- in question he was walking along Mere ileath-lane t\.??.wards Koutsford with a man named George Toft. , „ hen near the Squirrel Wood they heard two pistol •eota and a scream. Further on they saw Miss Francis, Ihd found the dead body of John Bould. Witness went t's the police. ~, MISS FRANCIS AND TH M E HORSEEN. .? George Craft gave similar evidence. George Henry Yarwood, wheelwright, of Dunham' sseY, deposed that he was out riding with Mr; Isritchard and a man named Rowe on the evening of : !th. Rowe ilismounted in Mere Heath-lane to speak' vv,saise Francis. and while he was talking to her witness' A"0 had gone *bead some seventy yards, heard four Of Pistol shots. Be saw no act of impropriety on the Pin of f Rowe. Tr kr Griffiths : And you were watching Rowe and Miss tttlancis the whole of the time P—l was not watching ern at all. 4ould you see anytaiing taking plaze between them could not, as I was going up the road. Yell didn't see him push her into the hedge ?—He °laid not have done. „,..rai also tell us that there was no act of impropriety? • id not see anything of the kind. you hear any screams P—No. t.t.rhen you heard the shots what did you do ?—I did do ,„"tbizg. oclr ffankes : if Rowe had used a revolver that night -1,14 You have seen it P—Certainly he didn't. ao..1:1 "Ply to other questions. Yarwood said they Were 4 the worse for drink. ROWE CALLED. livli,P.ero was another rustle of interest when George Eb,"laria Bowe was called. His evidence was very brief. p;'e!aid that he was remounting his horse when Miss bein",,,cle came up. fie made some remark about its tad a a wet evening, and then sprang on his horse and 0 off read. • Be had previously passed Miss Francis on the Griffiths (to witness) : Did you struggle with 0• —Certainly not. ig.acted improperly with her P—No. ,D ou hear her scream ?—No. Lbat a natural invention of hers ?—That I cannot It ja The !tot true ?—No. PeopinVrige : It is not only her evidence, but other GrierMr scream. : Did you hear shots ?—I didn't. when I did no: know any particular. I &ulna, see .the man nor the horeemen,and my evidence would not have helped them to find the murderer.
ANOTHER MAN.

Parrott also said he saw in the lane a miciale-3,v,d man wearing ajeit hat and an overco.t Mr Thomas: Was it a long overcoat?—Yes. Was it a dark brown one?—Yes. And yet you did not tell the police?—No. Did he wear spectacles?—No. Doyou suggest he did the murder ?—No, I do not. Mrs Parrott followed tier son in the boxand spoke to , repairing his purse, once,if not twice, by sewing it with cotton. She could show the places where bbe had stitched it, and could so regulate it as to stitch it in the holes where the previous thread had been: It was about ' last December when she first stitched it. Parrott's brother, John, remembered the accused coming home on Easter Sunday evening, and said that James did not seem to be at all excited—much the same aS usual, in fact. . SPEECHES OF COUNSEL.

A few minor witnesses having completed the defence, the afternoon was spent in liatening to the speeches of Counsel. Mr Griffith led off with his second address on behalf of the accused. Be said Heaven knew what happened in Mere Heath-lane at the time of the tragedy. There could be no doubt Parrott was there between Si% and seven o'clock, and his account of his movements was at any rate consistent, even if it was not confirmed by all the evidence that had been adduced by the prosecu- tion. There could be no doubt that the prisoner was in , the lane twenty minutes or half an hour before the 1 murder was committed, but there, counsel submitted, the process of identification was suddenly cut short. An attempt bad been made to identify the prisoner with the man who was seen leaning over the body. This I attempt had failed, but he ventured to say even if it had succeeded it would have been perfectly con- sistent with the prisoner's innocence. They must remember in connection with Miss Francis that she gave evidence of a certain kind which was seriously contradicted. Then, too they should bear in mind how the police had dealt with this girl. Did they, think it was necessary for the Chief Constable to go three times to visit a housemaid who was going to give evidence in this case ? If this girl was telling the truth there was no necessity for three visits from the Chief Constable and innumeraole visits from the sergeaut.who admitted that he only went to elicit evidence. They should remember that fifty yards away from the spot where this man was shot dead a woman was being violently ( assaulted for ten minutes, according to Miss Francis. Atter ten minutes of this sort of thing two shots were heard. Then, and not till then Miss Francis screamed That was one matter for the jury to ponder over. The prosecution made much of the tact that a purse was found in Parrott's box,and that a purse of the same kind had been used by Bould. If they believed the evidence of the prisoner's mother, who, true enough, was speaking for her own son, but who gave her evidence in a very fair manner, there was a complete answer to that. But even if they were not satisfied, he should contend that the prosecution had not proved that Bauld had such a purse in his pocket at any time imme- diately prior to his death. With regard to the coins they hitt' also a complete answer. There was really no motive to be ascribed to Parrott in the case. The theory of the prosecution was that Parrott committed the deed for plunder, afcer walking from Manchester, because he had no money. But the defence had proved that he had five shillings of his brother's money in his overcoat pocket, apart from what he might have had of his own. Was it not more likely that the murder was the work of some private enemy than of a man whose manner they knew was reserved, and who had only that very day declared that people who carried revolvers ought to be punished ? 'COOL AND BULL " -STORY

In his reply Mr Abel Thomas characterised as a cock and bull story the prisoner's explanation about the sale of the revolver to the sailor. The prisoner's explana- tions, he went on, teemed with improbabilities. There was a deep and mysterious suggestion, that there was some connection between the incident of Rowe and Francis and the murder? Where did it come from ? Did it come from the prisoner? Perhaps he could give some explanation. Or did it come from the ingenious brain of the solicitor instructing the defending counsel ? He ventured to think it did. Mr Thomas submitted that no other man than the prisoner could have been on the spot when the murder was committed. He sup- posed it was possible for anyone to have come across the field, but if there had been he would have been seen over the low fence.

THE SUMMING UP. Already the case had lasted much longer than bad been anticipated, and it was nearly five o'clock when Mr Justice Grantham commenced his summing up in a hushed and excited court. " One of the most extraor- dinary cases he had ever bad to deal with." was his Lordship's preliminary comment on the matter. Un- questionably, he went on, the evidence was of a purely circumstantial character, and none of the pieces of evidence taken by themselves were sufficiently strong to convict upon,although undoubtedly they did point more or less to the prisoner having committed the murder. The jury must exclude all elements of doubt from their minds before they said the prisoner was guilty. Al- though the evidence might point to the guilt of the prisoner, yet if there was a loophole to escape, or any time that had not been accounted for it would not be safe to find a verdict of guilty. It was impossible to remedy a mistake, and therefore juries should be very careful before they made up their minds adversely to the prisoner. There had been a good deal of evidence brought for yard which had really very little bearing upon the main issue, but he did not blame anyone, because in such a case the police did not know what evidence would be important.

TRIBONEIeSt,EVIDENCE UNSATISFACTORY. He had been very carefully through the evidence of the prosecution, and if the case had closed and the prisenerlhad not been called it would have been his duty to tell them that, although there was grave suspicion against the prisoner' it was not sufficient to justify them in convicting him of murder. But undoubtedly, now after the prisoner had given evidence, it was quite possible that the construction he had put on the evidence before might have been changed, and possibly their own opinion might,have beer% changed by the prisoner's statements. The prisoner's evidence, he was bound to say, was as unsatisfactory as it could possibly be. It did not appear to him to be consistent with truth, nor did anything that he said he did appear consistent with the actions of a rational and reasonable man. It was a remarkable thing that all the evidence which up to the 20th of April was most important to bring home the crime to somebody became useless in this Case, because the prisoner had admitted every bit of it. If they, therefore, erased the whole of this evi- dence,which the prisoner had admitted,and looked at the evidence for the prosecution that remained they would find there was scarcely any at all, and certainly not sufficient in his lordship's mind to justify them in con- victing him. TDB JUDGE AND ;COLT'S ADVERTLIMMENT. Parrott's explanation with regard to the disposal of the revolver, his Lordship continued, was most extra- ordinary. He was as startled as he was shocked that anyone from Colt's could demean themselves to such a low level as to advertise they would sell revolvers to cyclists, and induce cyclists 0 carry revolvers, when judges everywhere were asking the Legislature to do something to put a stop to the practice because af the lives lost and the people maimed. Here they bad in the teeth of all this makers advertising far and wide that they would sell revolvers to cyclists to shoot dogs or some such rubbish, an to do that they risked their lives and the lives of others. Just imagine the folly and wickedness of anybody riding about with a loaded pis- tol l Fancy anyone from Colt's being guilty of sending revolvers to cyclists ! His Lordship next referred to the prisoner's dealings with the sailor, and said it was rubbish. In coJclusion the Judge said the evidence called by the prosecution was undoubtedly very strong against the prisoner as far as probabilities were concerned, but it was not conclusive, because the prisoner had not been identified as having been seen with the murdered man, and again it.was only fair to say that so far as motiv was concerned a sufficient motive had not been estab tithed.

div.head: " NOT OVILTY.,
div.p: " NOT OVILTY.,

The jury were absent considering the case far about an hour. Confidently, as had been his demeanour throughout, the prisoner stood up to listen to the ver- dict. and a smile, as of fulfilled anticipation, was the only outward sign of the jay with which be received the foreman's words of " Not guilty." The decision seemed popular in the crowded court. There is just as mush room as ever for speculation as to what actually occurred when Bould met his mysterions death.
