div.head: VIADUCT INSTITUTE, EARLES-
div.p: VIADUCT INSTITUTE, EARLES-
TOWN.
Annual Meeting.

The annual general meeting of the members of tile Vim!tilt Institute, Eirlestown, was held in the large reading room on Wednesday evening. There was a very large attendance of members, over v Web Mr J W Emmett presided, supported by Messrs B Bailey, W Davies, J R Allen, P Connor, and T Ormand (secretary).
In opening the meeting, the chairman called upon the Secretary to itad the annual report of the committee, which stated as follows :

Ins:rms.—Although each member has, we hope ere this, received a copy of the balance sheet, we purpose. in: brief, referring to the main items of income and expendituie, in the hope that it will either stimulate discussiou, or prove there are no entries of a debatable nature. The actual income for the year is £392 Os 101 d being 211 103 3d less than for the year 1900. This decease is more than accounted for by two items. Hire of rooms, £5 103 and Apprentices' Premiums, £l2, but for your guidance we subjoin a summary showing six items of increased revenue amounting to £ll 93 81, and four explanatory of a decrease of £23 93 lid or a net decrease of £ll 10. 3d. BowaiNG.—For several years we have had to draw your attention to a falling off in the receipts from bowl. trig. This year, however,there is a substantial increase of £4 17s id. It is pleasing to record this augmentLd receipt but at the same time we beg to remind you that seven years ago the total revenue from bowling was, apart from the rent of No 3 Green, £25 so that there is still a shrinkage of nearly £3, which it was expected would be more than made up by the two handicaps,and the exceptionally fine weather. VISITORSVEEII.—You will observe from the summary of receipts just submitted that the Visitors' Fees this year are £2l us 3d or £2 lOs 3d more than for 1900. It is very gratifying to note this additional revenue, although it falls very far short of that for the year 1893, when the gate receipts realized the handsome sum of £3B.

EXPENDITURE.—The total amount expended is £362 03 11d. In addition to this £lO has been set aside on account of the expense which will very shortly be in. cursed in issuing a supplementary catalogue of tne books added to the Library since November 1894, and £2O has also been reserved for asphalting. A number of the walks, particularly those round Nos. 2 and 3 Greens,call for special attention and a very considerable outlay. Apart from these two items we believe there is nothing of exceptional nature, or requiring any explanation the whole of the die ursements. BAND.--la the two previous reparts we have had to lament the continued absence of the band from the In- stitute grounds. We are now pleased to state that either our criticism, or that of individual members, has had:the much desired effect. The band,as you are aware, has on several nights this season, played a series of beautiful selections in the Park, to the edification of a large number of delighted listeners. Another seasou we hope the Band Committee will arrange to play at stated periods during the summer months ; if this were done, a programme of the selections to be played could be printed and a copy given to each one corning into the grounds. The general public might also be admitted on these nights at the nominal charge of, say a penny. It is with more than ordinary pleasure we chronicle the fact that s.hout a fortnight ago the band known professionally as the Earlestown Via- duct Prize Band, took part in the 16th annual July brass band contest at Belle Vise Gardens, and was for- tunate in being awarded the third prize of £B,together with an eighteen guinea cornet and a silver medal. The Band Committee inform US that by virtue of their recent success they " have now won the coveted and indis- pensable qualifici.tion necessary to compete in the premier competition which takes place on the 2nd September." As an earnest of their good-will.and as an expression of hearty appreciation of what has already been, and it is looped will yet be, accomplished, the la- stitute Committee, at a meeting held on Monday last, unanimously voted the sum of ten guineas towards the expenses (which it is understood will be very consider. able) to be incurred in connection with the forthcoming competition. CONCERTS AND LECTtTRES.—A year ago we gave a resume of our efforts to institute a small charge rat threepence for admission to a concert held on the sth April 1900. In the discussion which followed the read- ing of the report, one member said " the committee should not be discouraged by the failure of their first attempt to regulate attendance at a concert by a small charge for admittance. Perhaps a system of reserving some seats might be tried. The fact that 150 did take threepenny tickets showed that that number would have been willing to pay if there had been a reserved section' of the hall." The suggestion was:not new to the commit- tee,for they hadlpreviousty considered the advisability of reserving a limited number of seats,and as the qaestion has been publicly ventilated, they believed the members would he fully alive to the advantages accru- ing to them from such a system, and that they would co-operate with the committee, and endeavour, by the purchase of tickets, to obviate those unseemly and dangerous crushes at the door which take place at every lecture and concert. The committee consequently determined to give the ticket question another trial,and eight days prior to the concert, announced for the 22nd Nuvember, 1900, decided to reserve 200 seats at sixpence each, the remainder of the seats being free. What was the result ? 59 only took " reserved seat " tickets.

The response, although anything but satisfactory, was nevertheless encouraging. So much so that it was again agreed to reserve the same number of seats for Villier's lecture on " Kruger and Khaki." The total sold on that occasion was 13. PARK TICKETS.—It may not be generally known that park tickets, avaiLible from the Ist April to the 30th September, are issued to non-members at a charge of 2s fid for the season. These tickets admit the holders to the grounds at any Gime and on any occasion within the period for which they are issued. Widows of deceased workmen are also granted park tickets free of charge, on application to the secretary. SECTIONAL REPRESENTATION.—The subject matter of truer and better representation than at present obtains was introduced for the first time last year. But as several of the new and enlarged shops are without their full complement of hands the time is not yet opportune for formulating such a scheme. The question will, how- ever. in due course, be again considered by your com- mittee. LIBRARY.—During the year ended the 30th June, 141 new books were added to the Library at a cost of £2B 2s 4, and may be classified as follows r—flistory, •bio- graphy and travels, 30; theology. 1 science and technology. 7 ; miscellaneous literature, g ; fiction', 97. The numbAr of readers for the year just closed is 312, as against 3EO for 1900, to whom 7,736 volumes were issued. The alight decrease in the number of readers, which we hope is transitional.may possibly be accounted for by an Increasing interest in the news-room, that Menu,' adjunct of all libraries. As the public meeting place was an essential of the small ancient denoocracies, so the essential of modern democracy is the newspaper. The public news-room, in a very great measure, makes the home newspaper reader, and in due time,if he is not already one, a reader of the current literature of the day. To this end y rur committee are ever alert, and as far as possible they select the best books, and those suited to the Varied requirements of the readers. It is said that a poor woman on seeing the sea for the first time WAS de- lighted. "It was grand," she said, "to see something of which there was enough for everybody." Well.there are books enough for everybody, and it is one of our privileges, as well as a serious responsibility, to make the access easy to good books. Sir John Lubbock, now Lord Avebury, in his " The use of Life," says "Books have been compared to friends, but among our living companions inexorable death often carries off the best. In books, on the contrary, time kills the bad, and prrri. lies the good." The Chairman said he need hardly Bay that the report which they had listened to was the very best they had ever heard in the hall, and was one which did the Secre- tary very great credit. He had touched upon almost everything that anyone could touch upon, and had left him the chairman very little to say. ge was pleased to hear that several improvements had taken place during the past year, but just bef3re going on to the accounts, he might say that he was glad to hear from the Secre- tary% report that the band had on several occasions come on to the Park, and as they had just heard, tea guineas had been voted to them by the committee. That only showed that when the band did anything for the committee, the committee were very willing to help them,and be was quite sure the committee would go on helping them, so long as they gave pleasure to the mem- bers of the Society. Mr Gilmour moved that the accounts be taken as read. The report was a very comprehensive and satis- factory one, except in one respect, and that was that the question of baths was not mentioned. He thought it was desirable they should have baths in connection with the Institute, and he should be delighted if the Chairman could bring the matter before the Directors, and bring about its accomplishment. Mr J Gee seconded, and it was carried.

ELECTION OF COMMITTEE. The Chairman declared the result of the ballot for the election of Committee-men, to be as follows .—T Worsley (813), W H Teece (790), G Bunting (750), C W Emmett (686), J R Allen (885), W Davies (671), J Bar- croft (604) ; the last mentioned to serve for one year, vice J Emmett, resigned. Messrs Liversage and Sephton were re-appointed audi- tors. Messrs J Gee and W Clare were re-appointed scrutineers. Mr J H Graham moved that a vote of thanks be accorded Messrs Anderton and Connor, who had retired, for their services as members of the Committee.—Mr A Bethel( sec.snded, and the vote was unanimously accor- ded. A vote of thanks to the Chrirmac, on the motion of Mr Gilmour, seconded by Mr Smalley, brought the meet- ing to a close.

div.head: Summing-up for the Opposition.
div.p: Summing-up for the Opposition.

the dense of Commons Committee resumed their consideration of the Manchester and Liverpool Electric Express Railway Bill on Tnnrsday last week. Mr Littler, KC, in summing up the case on behalf of the petition of the London and North-Western Raillay and Chesnire Lines, said the mono rail scheme was doomed to failure by its inherent defects. It was exceedingly c.mrplizated, . having five rails instead of two, and if for no other reason it was for that practically foredoomed. It was a significant fact that the system, although old, had been adopted on no practical railway as yet, except the Ballybunion line, which*was a ridiculous affair. The Americans, who were up to date in everything, and who seized on any new thing with money in it, had not even corisidered teri- ously the advisability of taking up the mono rail. He did not believe a single financier in the world would lay out a sovereign on a line such as that proposed. Why did Mr Behr take such a pathetic interest in the engineering progress of England. Why did he, a German, come to England to bless it with his mono rail. He suspected Mr Behr thought " John Bull is very rich, John Bull is very foolish and very apt to put his money into wild cat schemes, and sorne one gets the advantage." Why, he would like to know, if Mr Behr had such an interf st in Eogiand, did he try his experiments in Belgium ? He would like to point out that toose experimsnts were the only ones upon which the ManehL s:er ,tad Liverpool Committee had to rely. Mr Balfour Browne, replying on behalf of the promo' ters, submitted that it was unnecessary for the Com- mittee to consider very closely the details of the pro- posals, because the Board of Trade would not sanction the running of the line until they were convinced that it was absolutely safe, High speed could not be main- tained on ordinary railways going round curves, but on this line the highest speed would be maintained without danger. The invention was very simple. It merely resolved itself into the fact that the centre ot gravity was below the top rail. The greatest inventions were simplicity itself, and this invention being so simple was a great scheme that would revolutionise railway travel- ling.

div.head: Bill Passed.
div.p: The Bill Passed.

The Manchester and Liverpool Electric Express Railway Bill was passed yesterday by the House of Commons Committee. The scheme having already received the sanction of the House of Lords its adoption is now practically certain.

div.head: LONGEST STREET IN MANCHESTER.
div.p: THE LONGEST STREET IN MANCHESTER.

The late George Augustus Sala wrote a series of sketches entitled "Streets of the World." Among the streets described,was"Market-street,Manchester." This is °Le of the ,shortest,though the principal thoroughfare in Cottonopolis. The longest street in Manchester is Oldnam- street, which from its opening in Piccadilly opposite the Royal Infirmary, and after becoming "Oldham-road" a quarter of a mile distant, extends all the way to Oldham and through that important manufacturiag town. It is flagged and paved and bordered by houses and shops ' fora total distance of nine miles. To a stranger, woo could travel on a tramcar from Piccadilly to the further most point mentioned, unless made aware of the fact, would not know when he had left Manchester behind him and entered Oldham.

Among the hundred streets which branch offif rem this long route is Reattier-street, an important connection with the road that leads to Rochdale-road. A few doors from Oldham-road is the corner shop of Mrs Pickford, grocer and general dealer. According to toe Manchester Directory it is "No 7," and in this house a somewhat remarkable occurrence ,is reported. A boy of the district'put it crudely" There is a girl who lives there," be said, " what's turned yellow." The reporter interested in this astonishing report entered the shop and inquired for particulars, The " girl "in question is Miss Bertha Pickforci, Mrs Pickford's daughter and (according to her mothers admission) she had been afflicted about the close Of March, 1901, by a disease which changed the colour Of her skin to a pale yellow. The alteration was accom pulled by terrible pains in the head. She had now however, recovered, not only her original colour, but also her former robust health in a remarkably quick way, andjwhen our reporter called at the house he saw her, and took down the following statement "It is about three months ago that I became of a very bad colour. Life was almost unendurable. I was as yellow as that milk bowl which you see on the counter, and the pains in my head were terrible. I consulted a very clever doctor, and he told me I was suffering from anaemia. He prescribed for me, and I took his medicine for about sltc weeks. I admit that he did my head a little good, but on the whole I was almost as bad as I was before I went to him. I lost my appetite, and became weak and nervous. The least exertion tired me very much, and I became short of breath on walking only a short distance. My lips became pale and bloodless-looking, and many people remarked upon my sickly appearance." " I see you are quite well now. How was it brought about?

" A number of customers who frequent my mother's shop, seeing how bad I looked, continually suggested that I should try Dr Williams' pink pills for pale people, and I was induced to purchase a box." "And how long was it before you found any improve- ment in your condition " " I began to improve at once. I got better and better every day. The pains in my head gradually ceased; my natural colour returned ; and the shortness of breath arid tired feeling left me. I feel able for any exertion now.,,

"Bow many boxes did you take ? " "Only two boxes, but I was really cured with a box and a half. and I have not needed any since." "I suppose you have no objection to your name and address being published in connection with your cure?' " None whatever." Mrs Pickford, who was present during the interview, confirmed all that her daughterYisd said, and remarked that may people coming to the shop speak of Dr Williams' pink pills and the many cures they have effected.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
Wycliffe P.S.A. Society.

Mr William Beswick presided at the meeting of this society on Sunday afternoon and delivered a brief ad- dress based on the text " To you is the word of this salvation sent," Acts 13th chapter, 26th verse.—Mr J W Reader, ef Liscald denvered the address and brought grei tinge from the members of the Liscard P.S.A. Society. He proceeced to deliver a very helpful ad- dre,s on meeting trontees when they came.—Two solos " The Holy Vision" and" The Lost Chord," were very creditably given by Miss Summers. The service was also taken part in by Mr C Cotton, Air George Walling- ton and the Rev John Yonge (president). At the sug- gestion of the president it was decided to return hearty greetings to the members of the Liscard Society. The PreAlent also invited the members to co-operate with Ithe °facials in an endeavour to make an Effort to in- crease the membership at the beginning of the Septem— ber half year.

div.head: Missionary Services at Bold-street Wesleyan Church:
div.p: Missionary Services at Bold-street Wesleyan Church:

There were good congregatiens at Bold-street Wesleyan Church evi Sunday,when the Home Missionary anniversary services were held. The preacher was the , Rev William Potts, of Llandudno,a for mor superintend- lent of tile circuit. In the morning t hi= rev gentleman based his discourse on the words : " Ad the Apestles said unto the Lord, increase our faith." The choir rendered the anthem " Lift up your heads" (Hopkins), the organ being presided over by Mr Frank Hickman. At the evening service Mr Potts delivered an earnest sermon from the words "If any man thirst let him come unto Me and drink," &c. Another anthem, "The radiant morn bath passed away " was efficiently render- ed by the choir. Collections were taken on behalf of the Horne Mission Fund.—On Monday evening a public meeting was held in the chapel, Mr Joseph N Hartley presiding. There were also present on the platform—the Revs T Bishim, William Potts (Llandudno` and John Dugdale (Liverpool), the latter gentleman forming the deputation.—The Chairman remarked that what most struck him in looking thraugh the home mission annual report was the marvellous organization. The total in- come for 1900 was £44,000, and he was pleased to find that of that sum £8,600 bad been contributed by the juvenile society. It was marvellous that the juvenile association could collect more than opt -sixth of the total amount. He looked at the different districts and found. that the Manchester aud Liverpool district ccntriouted twenty per cent. (flear,hear.) When the 3 ming people encouraged the workers of home missions they need have no fear for the future. (Applause.)—The Rev T Bishop said the summary which the Chairman had just read was correct so far as the ordinary income was concerned. The income was £36,034, the expenses £36,678, and the defidiency £644, which would have to be added to the former debit balance of £6,740, which made a total liability of £7,384. They spent four times as much on foreign missions as they spent on home missions. With regard to the work that had been done, the report was very pleasant to read. It was a very encouraging report: They bad a special mission to fishermen at Stornaway and Fraserburg, which was conducted by Mr Josiah Nix. They had also twelve mission vans, and one of them was coming to the Warrington circuit in September, and they hoped to have it working in the country districts. It would stay with them from September to Christmas, and the conductor—Mr Hallam—had promised that if they made good use of it they could keep it until Easter. They had a Mission to Seamen the East London Mission, West, North, and South London Missions, the Central London Mission, and all were doing good work for the masses. The London and Shoreditch, and Manchester and Salford Missions also belonged to them. They had the Charles Garrett Mission in Liverpool, which was now undergoing a period of depression,but which would soon be coming out all right. They also had the Bolton, Birmingham, Leeds, Nottingham, Hull, Sunderland, Newcastle-on-Tyne, Bristol, and Edinburgh Missions. There were also Connexional Evangelists and District Missions. Last year the Warrington circuit contributed over £57. (Hear, hear and applause).—The Rev W Potts also spoke.—Mr Dugdale said that the borne mis- sion was synonymous with the term foreign mission, as in Christ's view there was no distinction. Mr Dugdale gave some interesting particulars of the work' of the home mission, and at the conclusion of his address was heartily applauded.—On the motion of the Rev T Bishop a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr Dugdals,Mr Potts, and the Chairman, for their services.—A collection was afterwards taken in aid of tbe hcme mission fund, and the meeting closed with the Benediction.

The lay public dearly love a The Sea Fight. sham fignt. To it the Volun- teer movement owed much 134tItits popularity in its earlier stages. Before the ack was made in extended order, and when •

the front did not require to cover a distance of twelve to twenty miles, a very fair idea of the snovements of the opposing forces could be got by the interested spectator, and the mêlée of blank cartridge was like music to the martial enthusiast. Altered conditions have somewhat modified the opportunity for observation, and reduced the spectator's pleasure in the same ratio, and those attending "Autumn Manoeuvres "have now to be content with seeing a very small portion of the fight. With the introduction of cycles into modern warfare the position of the poor pedestrian as specter has become increasingly difficult,and it will be complete if the latest proposal is carried into effect, and the motor-car, like the Roman chariot of old, is to take a part in the conflict between opposing armies. The same difficulties apply to a display of naval mimic warfare, only more so. The evolutions are on such an extended scale that the vision of the bodily eye is too restricted to take in a tithe of the operations. It is only through the eye of the mind that a glimpse can be obtained of the movements which are being made by the attacking and defending fleets respectively and fortunately the press correspondents with the several squadrons are keeping the public well sup- plied with materials with which to form the mental picture. Now that war has been declared the movements of the different vessels taking part in the operations in British waters will be carefully noted as they are recorded, and an effort made to appraise their value in effectiveness, as well as the skill of their commanders. So wide is the field of operations, however, and so involved the issues that it will not be known probably till the close of the manoeuvres, when the final adjudication has been given, whether our coasts have been ade- quately defended or whether we have fallen a prey to a foreign foe. The general platof the opera- tions is simple in itself. Fleet B, representing the British Navy, or that Dart of it charged with the defence of the United Kingdom— I which we may take to be the Channel Squadron has been warned that a hostile fleet —X— is making a descent upon the British coasts. The defensive squadron, which is cruising in the North Sea,has twelve battleships besides other craft, with coaling stations at Port - land, Plymouth, and Portsmouth. The enemy have only eight battleships, and they are lighter in tonnage; but they are faster, have more coal storage, and generally more modern equipment. They have obtained possession of Ireland and the Scilly Isles, where they have coaling stations. The eonditions have therefore been arranged as nearly as possible to correspond with what might be the positicin of this country under sudden invasion by a foreign enemy, taken at the worst and under a disadvantage. The hostile fleet starts operations from the Atlantic, and the "tug of war "will pro- bably take place in the neighbourhood of St. George's Channel. If Fleet B under the circum- stances should be able to hold its own and secure the defence of our coasts in safety, then we shall have reason to congratulate ourselves. If, on the contrary, Fleet X should prove victorious we shall atlleast obtain some useful experience of the fight- ing qealities of our ships, and perhaps learn some lessons that it may be well for our friends at the Board of Admiralty to remember and to improve upon for future occasions.

Our Volunteers are home again, looking browner I and better for their fortnight's camp on Salisbury I Plain. This has been their first experience of a brigade camp in company with regulars and under martial law' but they have acquitted them- selves so well that it is not likely to be the last. Martial law sounds rather important, but it makes practically no difference to the men—unless they misbehave. Then the difference would be very soon apparent. Misbehaviour was conspicuous by its absence, we are glad to say, and the battalions of the 30th Brigade, of which the Ist South Lan- cashire was one, earned high praise from the Brigadier-General, Sir Frederick Stopford. He ex- pressed himself as specially struck with "the great keenness displayed by everyone to make the most of the opportunities at Salisbury Plain for instruction in practical training in field duties and considering the few opportunities the battalions' have had prior to arrival in camp of working on ground suitable for manoeuvres he thinks the man- ner in which the training was carried out was most creditable to all concerned." This is gratifying recogn tion of the work done, and we think it may cionfidently be expected that the Warring- tons battalion's place iu the 30th Brigade is made secure.

There is a strong indictment in one of the maga- zines against what is called the passion for pace. We are told that all the resources of science are being utilised to aid the fondness for scurry, and thaethe one desire of rich and poor nowadays is to annihilate space. There is another side to that picture. Much of the eagerness to develop rail- ways, and to employ motor-cars, and quicken the use of electricity kr trams is really in the interests of repose. It is done in order to make the transit quick from the realm of traffic to that of rest. Who, for example, would wish to dwell by night as well as by day in the area of' disturbance of the cobbled streets of Leeds, when he can by quick locomotion get away to the hills ? It may be uncomfortable travelling for half-an-hour or more a day in a stuffy tramcar; but the value is obtained. At present the benefit of week-ends at the seaside depends largely on the individual. When the journey is a matter of only twenty or thirty miles the advantage is obvious; but until the mono-line is brought into practical use the good of a day-and-a-half at the seaside at the cost of a four or five hours' railway journey (reckoning coming and going) is not so certain. It depends on the temperament, and largely on the capacity for early rising on Monday morning. But, after all, it is absurd to pretend that people travel because they like it. Their only object is to make a complete change from their ordinary conditions, and to broaden their horizon.

Rnncorn Rural District Council was principally occupied on Tuesday in discussing the now notori- ous " Thelwall nuisance," which, by the way, is really in Grappenhall. Dr Penny, the expert who had been called in to help the Council to come to a decision regarding the nuisance and its cause, had presented his report. All the members of the Council had seen printed copies of the report prior to the ineeting,so that it was not surprising when, on the motion of Mr Linaker,the report was taken as being read. But it was surprising that the Council should decide to keep the report from the press, and not only surprising, tut highly im- proper. The public are the parties most concerned about a public nuisance like the one in question, and they are certainly entitled to hear what Dr Penny has to say on so important a matter. Why should the matter be kept secret P Because it contains allusions to some of the tanning processes in vogue at Messrs. W.Long and Son's yard? Surely not! That may be a suffi- cient reason from Messrs. Long's point of view, and no doubt it is, but it does not abrogate the right of the public to hear both the verdict in the case and the Judge's summing up. Instead, the people most concerned have to be content with a chance phrase or incomplete quotations from the report, as used by speakers at the meeting of the Council. This is very unsatisfactory, even though it is indicated that the nauseous smell comes from the tanyard. Possibly the Council will see wisdom ere its next meeting,as the adoption of the report has been postponed. It is quite certain that they will never end the Thelwall nuisance by a policy of secrecy and concealment.

div.head: EXA MINER FRIDA Y AUGUST 2 1901.
div.p: THE EXA MINER FRIDA Y AUGUST 2 1901.

The Knutsford murder has been a mystery all along, and the trial of James Crossley Parrott at Chester Assizes has not lessened the mystery one iota. Parrott, as everyone expected, has been acquitted, for there was nothing but the flimsiest of circumstantial evidence against him. There was not one fact which really connected him with the tragedy, except his presence in the neighbourhood at or about the time the deed was committed. Had he not given evidence on his own behalf he would have been acquitted just the same. In fact it is questionable whether the statement from his own lips did Par- rott's cause much good. His explanation had more than a few elements of weakness and improbability in it, but there was nothing to dis- prove what he said. It is generally believed that this young man is a hardly-used individual, for in addition to having the terrible charge of murder hanging aver his head he has suffered 14 weeks' imprisonment in Kuutsford Gaol with its con- sequent pemniary loss. There ought to be some method of compensating the unlucky mortal who is wrongfully charged and imprisoned, but there is not, except through the agency of kind charity. The murder itself looks as if it will have to be added to the long list of unsolved problems which is found in the annals of crime.

Local authorities bordering on Sankey Brook are being approached by the Lancashire County Council with a view to bringing about a much- needed improvement:in the condition of that filthy stream. It is certainly a case calling for imme- diate action. Too long have we been accustomed to hear the loud swelling chorus of complaints each recurring summer. There is every reason to believe that the brook is used as a convenient receptacle for the sewage of every authority which lines its banks. St Helens has been the greatest offender and unless steps are taken by the St Helens Corporation to prevent their sewage from entering the brook, it is very little use calling up- on the other authorities lower down the stream to stop the pollution. St Helens must be the first to act. The Warrington Corporation, we are sure, will be willing to make any sacrifice to cleanse the brook, but it would be useless expenditure unless the authorities higher up the stream did likewise. We believe it was the late Dr Goma' who pointed out that the residuals from the Gas Works which entered the brook tended to improve the brook from a health standpoint, rather than otherwise.

Since the departure of Shamrock 11. for American waters the interest in the coming yacht race has revived, and with it the hope that there will, after all, be a contest worthy of so famous a trophy as the America Cup. The quiet confidence which has been expressed by Sir Thomas Lipton— a confidence which is said also to be held in the most exalted quarters—has proved contagions,and a belief has sprung up that the challengi•er has been held in during the recent trials with the sister , yacht, and that a knowledge of her real capa- bilities is the secret possession of a few. The ex- pert yachtsman may laugh such an idea to scorn,but it has nevertheless secured a considerable hold on the public, aided, ne doubt, by a recollection of the singular precautions which were taken to prevent any information as to the model of the new Shamrock leaking out during the construction of the yacht. The feeling of renewed interest to which we have referred will naturally be stimu- lated by the intimation from the other side of the Atlantic that the Constitution is not justifying the expectations formed of her, and that notable alterations will be made in that yacht. This may only indicate a decrease of confidence quite natural on the approach of the important event, or it may show that the Defender has been as much over- estimated as the Snamrock 11. has, perhaps, been underestimated. At all events, the prospects of good sport when the yachts meet grow brighter, and the day of the first race will be eagerly awaited on both sides of the Atlantic.

Another gratifying report was laid before the shareholders of Parr's Bank, Limited, at the half- yearly meeting held at Warrington last week. The arrangement made by the directors whereby one meeting is held at Warrington each year affords country shareholders an excellent oppor- tunity of attending the meeting. Mr Dun, the general manager, characteristically described Warrington as the cradle of the old bank, and the large attendance of local shareholders betokened a continued interest in the company. Many in Warrington were associated with it in its early trials and the fact that the bank has risen to be one of thelmost influential in the country has tended rather to heighten the interest of War- rington people in the concern. To make a profit of £1f30,000 in six months, the whole of which, to use the words of Sir John Harwood, had been "honestly earned," is a triumph in banking and easily admits of a dividend of nineteen per cent. With such an excellent report before them it was not surprising that the shareholders were satisfied and the speeches resolved themselves into mutual congratulations.

The House of Lords Committee evidently does not think very highly of the objections to the Manchester Port Sanitary Authority which are raised brWarrington and Widnes on the principle of inclusion as contributory districts, for the pre- amble of the Bill was proved. Yet there could not, we imagine, be anything fairer and more equitable than the reason for Warrington's objection. The town does practically no trade with the Ship Canal and therefore derives no bene- fit from its presence in the neighbourhood. Yet it is called upon to pay a proportion of the ex- pense of the Manchester Port Sanitary authority based on the rateable value. Warrington's conten- tion was that this annual levy should be based on tonnage, which method would have resulted in those towns doing a profitable trade along the Ship Canal having to pay proportionately. The committee evidently thlnic that if Warrington has no shipping trade it is .Warrington's own fault,and the cultivation of that trade is Warrington's only remedy and set-off for the expense she will be put to.

The " professional " is always on the look out, and in trying to get at what was at the back of the desire for information of this kind, his fertile fancy would most probably suggest that some legacy for the lowly-born of the Board's particular locality was awaiting him. But one dis- agreeable thing which the Board in question has provei is, that a vast proportion of the tramps com- menced life in the rate-aided institutions at which, with their families, they still continue it from place to place.

Mr Justice Ridley can be credited with novel pronouncement in the scathing denunciation of betting which fell from his lips the other day at the Liverpool assizes. Mr Justice Wills had said very much the same kind of thing a few weeks pre viously. Nor have their lordships quite succeeded in enlightening the general public upon the most effective method of treatment of what is admittedly in very many provincial towns, one of the most complex questions of the day. The curse said Mr Justice Ridley must be remeditd in some way, and so say many others. But how? It is very well to expatiat-4 on an evil Viet is as obvious as anything can be, but it does not help us much. • The public look in vain for the " sovereign remedy." Even the evidence adduced before the Parliamentary Commission which is investigating the subject appears, for the most part, to be "stale, .it, and unprofltablervvhile the members of the Commission confess that they are without a practical suggestion as to the way in which the problem can possibly be solved. The simple Insistence that a remedy "must" be found is not enough as coming from learned judges, and if any one class of persons was thought more capable than another of off-ring some practical suggestion it shou'd su.elot be that of our judges. Next time one of them offers a vigorous denunciation it is hoped that he will have discovered what at ;east he con- siders a possible remedy. The public will only be too glad to give it due consideration.

There is, perhaps, nothing remarkable in the fact that the Parliamentary Committee of the Trades Union Congress is putting forward suggestions as to the course to be taken by Unionists in view of the decision of the House of Lords last week. It is little use for a lawyer, much less for a mere layman in such matters, to question the law of the House of Lords. Many people have been surprised at the ruling, whether sympathising with the spirit of the decision or regretting it. Most people have thought it fair in principle that a trades' union should be capable of being sued, but had no idea that the unions could be sued until the present decision, particularly as a few years since a bill was actually introduced—but met with such opposition that it was dropped—that would have expressly legalised that which the Lords now say was always legal. Trades unions may possibly now, attempt legalisa- tion with the object of repealing the Acts upon which the Lords relied, and, if they do, not a few politicians will find themselves embarrassed.

While agriculturists and owners of kitchen gar- dens have rejoiced at the splendid rains that have fallen, there was one man at least who could not be , expected to share in these pleasurable feelings, This was William Lockwood, the famous Surrey cricketer. He was to have received a well-earned benefit from the proceeds of the Surrey and York- shire match, but not a ball was bowled on any of the three days, and the loss to Lockwood is esti- mated At .£7OO or £BOO. The Surrey club is, how- ever, a wealthy organization, and will scarcely allow the great professional to suffer to this extent through the caprice of English weather. By the bye, the action of the Yorkshire Committee :n pass- ing a resolution expressing a wish that Wilfrid Rhodes should not accept Mr Haclaren's invitation to accompany his team to Australia, adds one more to the cricket crisssiof the present season. For the Yorkshire Club, being very strongly supported by a sport-loving community, has always been able to ensure that when a man renders good service to the county he shall be left well off, and the " wish " of the committee under all the circumstances is very like a mandate, which, for Yorkshire cricket and his own sake, his friends trust he will accept in the spirit in which it has been given.

div.head: MATTERS OF MOMENT. A Provincial Letter.
div.p: MATTERS OF MOMENT. A Provincial Letter.

A great deal more interest has been manifested by the farming and agricultural communities of the provinces than one had ventured to hope as the result of the debates at the recent British Congress on tuberculosis. And a still further result has been that in thdllouse of Commons on Tuesday evening the President of the Local Government Board announced the consideration by the Government of the advisableness of appointing a Royal Commiesion. to inquire into and report upon the communicability of bovine tuberculosis to the human species. But the fact remsins that we have already had a Tuberculosis Commission, which assumed such com- municability to have been proved. That assump- tion has now to be set aside, but it will not do to embark on the new investigation in any biased frame of mind. The desideratum is absolute im- partiality. Dr Koch says his experiments have satisfied him that bsvine and human tuberculosis are two distine, diseases, and that they cannot possibly proceed from a common origin. His hypothesis is, of course, opposed to all theories hitherto accepted in this country. That, however, is no reason why, having regard to the weight of Dr Koch's authority, all his argument and data should not be very carefully considered by a scien- tific and perfectly unbiased tribunal.

Here is something for British out-of-works, of I whom there always appear to be an abundance, summer and winter, and in every potsible kind of weather or state of the labour market. Thousands of labourers are said to be required to harvest the crops in Canada, which have been particularly and marvellously abundant this year, and the Canadian authorities ask that efforts be made on this side of the Atlantic to supply the demand. div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
MUSIC FOR TFIE PEOPLE.

On Saturday the weekly open-air concert was held in connection with the Mersey Mission to Sea- men, in the recreation field, in the llolloway, Run- corn. There was rather a poor attendance. A good programme of music was gone through by St Edward's Catholic Band, Sports of all kinds were indulged in with great spirit.

div.head: : NEW FORM- OF IiETENGE AT WIDNES.
div.p: A : NEW FORM- OF IiETENGE AT WIDNES.

At the Widnes Sessions on Thursday morning, before the Mayor, Peter O'Toole, a hard-working man, living at 2, Witt-road, was charged with breaking a window at the police-station, value 108. Police-Constable Messenger said he was on duty at the station when prisoner came by, and, covering his hand with the end of his coat sleeve broke the window. He pleaded guilty, and, on being asked why he had done this, isaid, "I have had trouble at home, and want to go to gaol," Prisoner was fined 10s damage, 3s and costs, or fourteen days in default.

div.head: NEW CLERGYMEN FOR WIDNES.
div.p: NEW CLERGYMEN FOR WIDNES.

The trustees of the Widnes livings have filled up the two vacancies by appointing the Rev George Stephen Jones, 8.A., to St Mary's and the Rev Douglas E Morton to St Paul's. Mr Jones gradu- ated with Theological Honours at Pembroke College, Oxford. For the last five years he has held the senior curacy of St Aldates, Oxford, under Canon Christopher. Previously he was curate at Great Yarmouth, under Canon Rogers, and at St Paul's, Stratford, under the Rev D J 8 Hunt, the successor of Canon Hoare at Holy Trinity, Tun- bridge Wells. Mr Morton was educated at St John's, Highbury,and is at present senior curate of St Leonard's, Bootle.

div.head: SALVATION ARMY, HIGH-EITRRIIT
div.p: SALVATION ARMY, HIGH-EITRRIIT

On Sunday flower services were held, celebrating the 36th anniversary of the world-wide Army. The meeting at night was well attended, many fresh faces being present. The service was of a novel character, speakers being chosen for the occasion, namely, W Chadwick, treasurer; J Worrell, Ser- geant Major ;Mr and Mrs Cameron,soldiers, who all spoke well on various topics. The peaking was interspersed with singing and solos corresponding with topics used. Captain Young, who is in charge of the work, at the close gave a powerful and tell- ing address, basing his remarks on the 16th Chapter, of Mark and 16th verse. The Hall was beautifully decorated with flowers, which have been distribu- ted amongst the sick people of the town. PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHURCH, RUNCORN.

The annual choir sermons were preached on Sun- day. In the morning the pulpit wag occupied by the Rev .1 Osborne, M.A. Special hymns were ren- dered, and the anthem, " Praise the Lord 0 Jeru- salem," received excellent treatment, the accom- panying duet being feelingly interpreted by Misses Davies and Rillidge. In the evening the preacher was the Rev W A Eyre, superintendent of the cir- cuit. The anthems were "Sing unto the Lord," and "Bless the Lord omy soul." Mr A Shingler was entrusted with the solo in the latter piece, and the quartette was taken by Misses S A Stubbs and 0 Stubbs, and Messrs T !Midge and J Stubbs. The solo in "Sing unto the Lord " was rendered by Mr A Woodward. These were efforts of high merit, and the general opinion was that the musical por- tion of the service was of all round excellence. Mr W Gittens' manipulation of the organ contributed in a large measure to this satisfactory result- The collections showed a slight increase on those of last year.

div.head: LOCAL POLICE CHANCIER.
div.p: LOCAL POLICE CHANCIER.

At the conclusion of the ordinary business of the Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, Mr A it Nor- man, the presiding magistrate, referred to the forthcoming departure from Runcorn of Superin- tendent David Pearson, consequent upon his pro- motion to first-class superintendent, and his transfer to the Middlewich Division. He said they commended the way in which he had carried out his duties as the superintendent of the Runcorn Division. He had performed those duties in a very satisfactory manner, and he was sure they all hoped his removal from Runcorn would be for his benefit. Mr Prichard (Mr Norman's colleague on the Bench), said Superintendent Pearson left the town with the goodwill of everybody. Superintendent Pearson, in reply, said it was vary gratifying for him to know that his services had been appreciated during his short sojourn in the Runcorn Division. He bad always tried to do right In the discharge of his public duties, and he was pleased to say that he had always received Ile greatest courtesy from the magistrates. As long as he lived he should never forget Runcorn for the kindness and sympathy shown to him on one par- ticular occasion. The circumstances were well known to the Bench. He was very much obliged to them for their kind expressions on the present occasion., It was with a pang of regret that he had to part with his old friend Mr Johnson, whose counsel from time to thus had been invaluable. He only hoped he might meet with the same courtesy end assistance in his new sphere of labour. Mr Johnson congratulated the Superintendent on his promotion, and wished him every success. ANNUAL MASONIC PICNIC /FROM RUNCORN.

• About 40 ladies and gentlemen- connected with ' the Ellesmere Lodge of Ancient Free and Accepted Masons,bad their usual annual trip on Thursday last week. The place originally decided on was Rnyl, but owing to unforeseen circumstances the com- mittee who had the arrangements in band even- tually decided that Southport would be a more suitable place. Crossing the Runcorn Bridge .the party were met by conveyances at the Widnes side, nd conveyed to the Central Railway Station, arriving, after one or two stoppages, at their desti- nation a little after mid—day, After spend- ing some little time in the town the party proceeded to the Prince of Wales Hotel, where an excellent dinner had been provided by the host. The usual masonic toasts closed the repast, after which two large convey- ances were requisitioned to convey the party to the seat of Lord Lathom,who had very kindly consented to throw his grounds open for inspection. Unfor- tunately the weather was of such a character that it was deemed advisable not to make a prolonged stay, and the homeward drive was commenced amid a downpour of rain, which militated con- siderably against the success of the trip. After a drive of at least 20 miles the company returned to the hotel,where an equally substantial tea had been prepared. After a short stay in the town the return :journey was made, Runcorn being reached by the same route about ten o'clock, after a most enjoyable day. The committee who had the arrangements in hand were the past masters and the three senior officers of the lodge, though to Bro T H Annett, secretary, and the W. SI., Bro C E Hicks, must be attributed much of the success of the picnic.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES.
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES.
--- [BY A CORRESPONDENT.]

-- The alleged nuisance at Tholsvall was the princi- pal bone of contention at the RULICOTII Rural Dis- trict Council meeting and for some IS months it has been on the boards and got no " forrader." With the merits and dismerits of the case of Messrs Long and Son and Mr Naylor I have nothing to do. Butt do wish to most emphatically disapprove of the action of the Rural • District Councillors in the matter of with-holding Dr Penny'fa report from the 'public press. This is surely not the correct way of letting the public get to the bottom of it. It has come to my ears also that the Press representatives who attend Dutton Workhouse are said to have been" got at," and they are accused (falsely I know) of unfairness in the matter. But the ; peculiar part of the business is bbat almost the 'identical persons who attribute this unfairness to the reporters willingly agree to withhold such a cogent report as that of Dr Penny.

--- Wednesday last was celebrated as the annual trip day of the St Michael's,St John's and Camden Sunday Schools. The two former in accord with customary practice 'visited the Frodsbam Hills, whilst the latter spent a most enjoyable time in a field adjoining Crofton Lodge. In the evening the town was quite gay everyone abroad being attired in full holiday regalia.

The statements of the Iturworn Rural District Council, and the Runcorn Urban District Council just published form very interestino reading. As they appear elsewnere in this journal comraent is unnecessary.

Referring here to Admiral Jones Parry's "inter- esting book on Workhouse Management," which he so ably championed at the meeting of the Board of Guardians on Tuesday, I might say that the edition quoted was issued in 1870. 1 only hope the "two" the Guardians will have to guide them will be of more recent issue.

--- Runcorn Heath and Runcorn Hill are now the I property of the town, The District Council is rapidly transferring the hitherto 'wilderness" into a delightful spot, and I feel sure the members will have the co-operation of the inhabitants in their undertaking. On Bank holiday (Monday next), there is to be an interesting model yacht race on the lake, arid no doubt numbers of people will avail themselves of the opportunity of witnessing it.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.

The usual fortnightly meeting of this body was held at the Workhouse, Dutton, on Tuesday, Mr Joseph Knowles J.P., presiding. There were also present:— Admiral Jones Parry, Messrs S Woodward, J Mclntyre, T Wright, J B Chadwick, C E Linaker, J Moseley Williams, J Taylor, T Darlington, E A Waliington, G Pilling, P Gleave, J Spruce, T Lewis, J Whitlow, H Mawdsley, A G Guest, W H Bradford, A Eaton, R Billington, with Mr George F Ashton (clerk), Mr W E Hough (assistant clerk), Messrs Diggle and Swinton (surveyors), Mr James Farrington (inspector), and Dr J Adams (medical officer.)

div.head: SPECIAL EXPENSES.
div.p: SPECIAL EXPENSES.

The Assistant Secretary of the Local Government Board wrote stating that the Board would proceed to issue an order declaring the remuneration paid by the Rural District Council of Runcorn to their surveyors for services rendered to the Parochial Committee of Prod- sham, Frodsham Lordship, Helsby and Stockton Heath, for the year ended on the 31st March last, to be sprcial expenses chargeable upon the contributory place con- cerned.

div.head: WARRINGTON AND THE =ELWELL WATER SUPPLY.
div.p: WARRINGTON AND THE =ELWELL WATER SUPPLY.

Mr John L Whittle, Town Clerk, Warrington, in a letter with regard to the Thelwall Water Supply said he was instructed to state tbeE his Council would be pre- pared to extend the main for supplying the Township of Thelwall with water on having a guarantee from the Runcorn Council on the basis of an agreement enclosed. He understood that the statutory charge of 6 per cent. on the ratable value of the premiers requiring a supply of water was sufficient to cover the guarantee ef 8 per cent. on the cost of the main.
On the proposition of Admiral Jones Parry, second d by Mr Gorge Pilling, it was decided to give the necess- ary guarantee. _

lINIFORDE BYE-LAWS. A question arising with regard to some Building Bye- laws, in the Parishes ot Stockton Heath, Fr odsham and Weston Mr J 3 Chadwick gave notice be would submit a motion, with the object of having uniformity in the matter throughout the District, at the next meeting. THE " THELWALL NUISANCE." DR. PENNY'S RE"ORT WITHHELD. The Clerk intimated that the report of Dr Penny, re - garding the &Beged nuisance at Thelwall, was to hand. A copy had been sent to each member of the Council. Was it requisite that he shoirld read it again ? Mr Linatter considered it was not desirable that the report ehould go to the papers. They could take the report as being read. This was agreed to. The Clerk stated his reason for putting the question I was the following letter received from Messrs Long and ISon Grappenhall,Warrington, July 26,h, 1901. George F Ashton, Esq , Runcorn. Dear Sir,—We beg to enclose you a copy ot our letter to Dr Penny after reading his report, and we cannot more fully express our views to you about the promise your representative gave as res. rooting all the details we gave him. We think you must recognize the unfairness to ourselves of circulating these reports. Willing as we have been to give your Board every assistance in our power, we cannot stand to be shot at in this manner, and we must protect our own interests, and those of such an old established business against such damage which may occur to us through the publication of statements which are incorrect. You will no doubt recognize the seriousness of the case, and we trust will either call in the reports, or at all events prevent such being allowed to appear in the newspapers. We hir,•,e to furnish you shortly with a report from the highest authority we have been able to obtain respecting the charges made against us, and will leave your Board to draw their own conclusions. In the meantime we remain yours truly, Wm. LONG & SON." The following was the letter referred to :—Grappen- hall, Warrington, July 22 id 1901. Dr PennY.Aldershot. Dear sir,—We have been favoured with one of your printed reports in reference to our yard and need hardly say with what surprise we read the particulars you give respecting:the process and working of our business, after your distinct promise that such should be treated as confidential and used only to assist you in making your analysis. It is we consider nothing more or less than a distinct breach of privilege after our interview and inspection when we gave you every possible assist- ance and.told.you the books even Were at your disposal

if you wished. We have always shown ever's, disposition ,to assist the District Council or their representatives whenever they have been to inspect the yard, and if you consider it right to put into print and distribute as you think fit the private details of our business we do not, and may say that we shall hold you responNible if such is made public property especially as some of the facts are incorrect and not as given by us. To give your analysis of the .ffiuent is of course quite in order whether good or bad and that we have no objection to, but for the rest we consider we have been imposed upon under false pretences. You do not,we notice,think it necessary to say what our neigh- bours' sewage consists of and give a detailed account of the working of hie household,then why make an exception and take advantage of the privilege and assistance we gave you? We can place only one construction upon it. As the report was not read at the last Board meeting, and the next is not until the 30th inst., we thought it best to express our opinion to you before such time. We remain, yours truly, William Long and Soo." Mr Linak Was there any reply from Dr Penny,or a letter from bin.

The Clerk : I am coming to that. Dr Penny also forwarded a copy of the letter received by him and the following letter Ro The!wall Nuisanee.—South Western Hotel, A.lder- shot, July 25th, 1901. To the Runcorn Rural District Council. Dear Sir, Received the enclosed letter from Messrs Long and Son, which I considered it my duty to place before you. In reference to the allegation stated therein I may say that nothing was given 0 me in con- fidence, and all the facts detailed in my report came to me in my official capacity, and in that alone. I con- sider that I was not only entitled to use such Informa- tion afforded me, but I should have distinctly failed in my duty had I withheld any such information. I must ask your Board to deal with the letter in such manner as they deem fit. I have informed M,ssrs Long k Son that I have forwarded this letter to you. Kindly ac- knowledge receipt. Yours truly, John Penny, M.B.— To George F Ashton, Esq., Clerk. Mr Moseley Williams : Have the Local Government Board received anything from you ? The Clerk: We have not sent anything to the Local Government Board although they asked to be furnished with a copy of Dr Penny's report as soon as published. It has not been before you in an official way until to- day. Mr Linaker pointed out that the Council bad gone to the expense and troubln of appointing Dr Penny to draw up a report on the matter for them. It seemed to him that the gist of the report was in the last paragraph, wherein Dr Penny says: '6 Undoubtedly at times, an offensive effluvium nuisance injurious to health arises therefrom." It was the very thing they bad asked their own Medical Officer to report upon as to whether the nauseous efltuvia were injurious to health or not. They were now told it was.
voti:

dr Mclntyre: Are you, Mr Chairman perfectly sate. fled as to where the nauseous smell arises P Mr Linaker : If we put the right construction on the report we cannot have any doubt as to where it is alleged to come from. And, if you ignore the report, we are in the same place as we were before. The Chairman, in reply to Ur Mclntyre : According to Dr Penny's report, it comes from the tanyard. Any- way, I read it so. Mr Woodward : If you adopt this report you assert definitely and clearly that "No doubt, at times an offen- sive, disagreeable nuisance injurious to health arises from the effluent from Messrs Long's Tannery." That is practically in the last clause. I have only changed the wording a little. If you adopt the report you assert there is a nuisance injurious to health. If the same arose on any farm, or on a place in town you would ask the people to abate the nuisance by serving them with notice to the effect, and the people would have an oppor- tunity of either proving there was no nuisance, or given time to remove the same. That would be the proper course to take with regard to Messrs Long and Son. (Haar, hear). Mr. Mclntyre then criticised several items of the report (to record which would be unintelligible without the whole) and wound up by producing a sample of an effluent he bad taken from the twelve inch pipe in Waste-lane. Be should like to ask the Chairman or any other member to smell it and see whether it was such an effluent as reported on by Dr Penny. (Laughter.) The bottle was passed to the front.

Mr Piling : Have you a glass (increased laughter.) Mr Linaker took it the Council was considering Dr Penny's report, and not any samples as taken by Mr Mclntyre. Mr Mclntyre : Then Ibe your pardon and will take that mjew• Mr Wallington : Is Waste-lane the principal road in Thelwall A Voice Yes. Mr Wallington : [fit is so, does not the sewer belong to the authority? Mr Mclntyre : Then I say it is the authority who is guilty of the whole offence. Mr Mounfield rose to nropose that the report of Dr Penny be received and adopted. Mr Linaker seconded. Mr Woodward proposed that the report be not yet received. Mr Linaker : A. direct negative. Mr Woodward : The report can only be fairly con- sidered by experts. They had their own Medical Officer (Dr Adams),--equally qualified with Dr Penny, and he contended they should give their Medical Officer an opportunity of either confirming or other- wise expressing an opinion on Dr Penny's report. Otherwise they were accepting the opinion of one man without any confirmatory evidence. Mr Darlington supported Mr Woodward' s views. Mr Wallington referred to the urgency of the case and to tho fact that there was still sicknas in the house owing to the alleged nuisance. - Mr Linker contended he bad always bald there own Medical Officer was the tierSol3te .etl w,411.0:kt matter,

and referred to the fact that it was only the difficulty of getting his expression of opinion as to the alleged nuisance being injurious to hsalch, that resulted in his voting for the services of Dr Penny. He felt it would be an insult to Dr Penny to now disregard lois report. Dr Adams than characterised the report of Dr Penny as in direct agreeinent with his first report on the sub. ject submitted some 18 months previously. The efflu- ents were of a varying character. The only material difference in Dr Penny's report and his own appeared to be the controversial question as to whether it was re- sponsible for zymotic diseases. There did not appear to be any evidence in the report to show such was the case and it was only stated as Dr Penny's opinion. Subsequently a vote was taken and Messrs Wrigh:, Linakpr, Wallington, Lewis, William*, Mounfield, Tay- lor, Whitlow, Parry and Baxter (10) voted for the adop- tion cf the report ; and Messr,, Woodward, Mclnt) re. Darlington, PilLing, Spruce, Bradford, Gleave, Mawds- ley, Billington and Guest (10) against. The Chairman than gave his casting vote in favour of adjourning vestion. The • reports on the Rocksavage nuisance and an improvement at Sutton were considered satisfactory and confirmed.

At four o'clock on Monday aft-qn-oon, a parte named William Rowlinson, who is 55 years ot age, and lives in Greenell-street. was crossing the line in front of a train at the Central Station. He failed to clear the lines and a wheel of the engine went over his foot, severely crushing it. Rowlinson was taken to Vie infirmary, w•lere the injured foot wan amputated. Junior Swimming Handicap, Prior to the commencement of the dye-ton v Warrington water polo match at the Corporation baths on Tueqclay evening, a fifty yards junior Swimming Handicap was decided. There were ten competitors and the final hest proved very inV?resting S Ince gained first position with a load of about two yards, whilst A Barnes an J Rath- bone tied for second place. Rathhone and Barnes tried conclusions a second time with the same result. The prizes consisted of handsome medals. Girl Run Over at Stockton Heath. At 11-30 on Wednesday morning, a little girl learned Maggie James, daughter of George James, 116, Greenall's-avenue, was run over near the Swing Bridge, Stockton Heath. It appears that she was crossing the road near the bridge when a spring cart, belonging to Thomas Muskett, wheelwright, Whitley, which was being driven by his wife, knocked her down A wheel of the cart passed over one of the girl's legs, but fortunately no bones were broken and no other serious injuries were sustained.

St Peter's Men Service.—Trip to Gateacre. Last Saturday afternoon the members of the St Peter's Church Men's Service had their annual ex- cursion to Gateacre. 'Buses, supplied by Mr H Greenough, left the schools in John-street about two o'clock, and the drive, although a long one,was thoroughly enjoyed by the party, which numbered about forty, and included the Kv B Percival (vicar), the Rev W Bracecamp, and Messrs T S Steel, Pater Edgar, W Bay and others connected with the church. . Gateacre was reached shortly hetore five o'clock, at which hour a substantial knife-and-fork tea was provided at the Black Bull Hotel. The repast was excellently served, after which an adjournment was made to the grounds of Colonel Walker, The Grange, who had kindly given permission for the party to make an inspec- tion of his well kept and well stocked gardens and conservatories. The head gardener showed the visitors the many beautiful plants and Rowers. A thorough inspection having been made and much enjoyed the party broke up to spend the remainder of the evening in various ways. Some rambled round the lanes to view the many pretty house gardens to be found in the vicinity. Others enjoyed names of bowls on the green attached to the Bull Hotel. The return journey was commenced about eight o'clock, Warrington being safely reached at 10-45. Excellent arrangements bad been made by the Rev W Bracecamp and Mr T S Steel.

A Local Regiment and its Recruiting. A Liverpool contemporary says :—The decision of the War Office to merge the new 3rd and 4th Battaliotts (Regulars), of the King's Liverpool regi- ment into the Ist and 2nd, will, of course, seriously check the flow of promotion in the professional units of The King's. Otherwise the reversion to two battalions is not to be regretted, it being ohvious that a couple of strong units are fax more effective than four, of which three are reduced to skeleton elements to maintain a heavy establish- ment. The four battalions are.very full of officers, and no doubt transfers to other regiments will be found for some. As a whole the four line battalion system has not worked satisfacterily, especially when three have been on home service. The failure to recruit the regiment up to the expected number is not surprising, but it is somewhat regrettable that a larger proportion of Liverpool regular in- fantry enlistments are for other regiments than that nominally identified with the City. The King's (Liverpool Regiment) would probably fare in this respect better were it connected with a single rather than a double depot and had its regimental district home in this citT rather than in Warrington.

While the Judges' carriage was proceeding from the Assize Courts at Liverpool to Newsham House, where the Judges lodge, on Monday evening, a lady cyclist rode out of a side street and was rue over by the carri- age, which was occupied by Mr Justice Ridley, Mr Justice Bucknill, and the High Sheriff. Tha wheel went over the lady's chest, and she appeared to be consider- ably hurt. The Judges sent a doctor to attend her at her home.

A strike has been ordered at the San Francisco docks. Some 55,000 men are idle, and business is temporarily suspended. The Paris-Lyons Railway Company has just purchase 50 Anaerican steam engines, which will cover the dig. tance between Paris and Marseilles in ten hours instead of thirteen, the time taken at present by the fastest expresses.

On Tuesday afternoon at Marlborough House, the King conferred upon Mr T Sydney Cooper, RA., the dignity of a knighthood of the Victoria Crder. His son. Mr Neville Cooper, was als3 presented to his Majsaty Sir Sidney Cooper's health is now mach better.

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
CRUELTY TO HORSES.

At the Borough Police Court on Monday morning several persons were charged before Mr Monks (in the chair) and other magistrates with cruelty to animals, In the first case the defendants were Ralph Hope, of 60, Bold-street, Leigh ; and Thomas Pickles, also of Leigh, the former being charged with illtreating a horse while it was in an unfit tato and the latter with causing it to be so worked.—lnspeotor Print, RSPC A, said be ex- amined the animal. It was suffering from a sore. The driver said he was perfectly innocent that anything was ' the matter with the animal. Subsequently witness saw Pickles and he admitted that he knew the animal was suffering from the sore, and he added that he would "take the conaequences."—Each defendant was fined 7, 61—Robert Shaw. 8, Mary-street,Moas Bank.Widnes, was also summoned for having on the 15th July Unseat- ed a horse by working it whilst it was in an unfit state, and Andrew liegarty, who gave the same address, was charged with causing the animal to be worked. Inspector Print said that on the 15% July he was on duty in Factory-'ane, Bank Quay, when he saw Shaw driving a bay horse attached to a trolley which was empty. The animal wla very lame. Shaw was fined 5s and Hegarty 53 and costs.—John Wilkinson, of Grappenhall, and Joseph Fairhurst, also of Grappenhall were charged with a similar offence.—Mr. Browne represented defendants. Inspector Robinson prosecuted and said be was on duty in the Fair Ground at Warrington, when he saw defendant Wilkinson in charge of a mare The animal was very lame on the off fore leg and he r xamined it. The leg was also very badly sprained; the fetlock joint was badly sprained and the joint was "knuckling over." The animal was in very great pain and usfit to travel any distance. Shortly afterwards witness saw Fairhurst, who said he had sent Wilkinson with the horse. He knew it :was lame, but it was not so bad As it was at that particular moment. It was his antentfilla to have it destroyed and eventually the animal was killed:—Mr Browne: Don't you thick the killing of the horse was a sufAcient loss without bringing the case into Court ?—lnspector Robin- son: No one can tell where the animal would have gone to. It might have gone to Germany. Further ques- tioned by Mr Browne Defendant Fairhurst said he wished he had had the animal killed ae, home„ as it was an old favourite, and witnesa told him it was only fit to be slaughtered. The society wished to stop this kind of traffic with horses.—lnspector Print also gave evidence. —Mr Browns, for the defence, said the defendant was a highly respectable man and was a wheelwright and blacksmith at Grappenhall. He had had this particular horse for seven years and it bad a " pottering gait." It had gone to Warrington three or four times each week during that period, and a month ago it sprained itself with the result that Fairhurst kept it up for a few days and then sent it out to do light work. When the horse started it "knuckled over" two or three times, and after that it went as well as any other animal. In Fairhurst'a opinion there was no cruelty at all. He had severallilwitnessss to call, /including Mr John Griffiths, tenant of the Cheshire Cheese lan, Latehford, who would say that they had seen the animal walking all right.—At this stage, however, the magistrates stopped the cage.—lnspector Robinson seeing that they were about to give a decision, said he would be satisfied if the Banda fined defendant in the costs. The society was anxious to put a stop to this kind of thing.—Mr Browne: You are constantly talking about " put a stop to it." This is the first time a similar charge has been brought against my client.—Mr Monks : It is for us to decide what the fine shall be. The man has lost his horse, and under the circumstances we have decided to dismiss th 3 A FATHER'S INHUMAN CONDUCT. At the Warrington Police Court on Thursday, before Mr John Fairclough (in the chair) and other magistrates James Rowlinson, 3, Mill-yard. off Fennel-street, was charged on a warrant with assaulting and illtreating his son Alfred on July 29113.—Mr A Browne prosecuted on behalf of the NSPC C. and said the boy was 'Mayen years f age. On July 29th the boy tame into the house with hie jacket wet. Prisoner, who was drunk, thrashed him with a strap and hit him across the eye with a buckle. Prisoner had previously been before the Court for neg- lecting bis family, and served 14 days' imprisonment. Be would not work, and but for the earnings of an e"elder son the family would have been starving.—Mrs ^Rowlinson was called and said her husband had neglec- ted the family for some time past. If he choose to work he could earn 30s per week.—Poliee Sergeant Bell stated ; that on the date in question the boy came to the Police ,Station. He was crying and blood was streaming down sehis cheek.—Prisoner was sent to gaol for a month with bard labour.

• ...FRIDAY —Before His Worship the Mayor (Alderman Roberts) in the chair. Alderman Monks, Councillor John , Roberts. 3 Hepherd, and H Thornton. Eithuor WITH A CLOG —Bridget Wheeler. Jolley's Court, was summoned for assaulting Mary McCormick. 7. Brick- .r -street on July 20th.—The complainant and her husband and r a neighbour named Sarah Clare deposed that the defendant struck the complainant with a clog on the forelsead.—The defendant denied this.—The magistrates fined her in the costs. 13s A BUCKET OF SITDS FOR THE RENT COLLECTOR--Catherfne Relly.2 Smiths Court,was summoned on a charge of assault- ing Thomas Cowdell. rent collector, 31, Legh-street on July 22nd.—Mr Fowler represented Mr Cowdell and stated that to on the date named his client served the defendant with ore notice to quit. She used insulting language to him and as he was leaving the door she threw a bucket of soap suds over him. The defendant had since called at the complainant's house and he agreed to withdraw the case if she paid the cost of the summons and left the house. That morning she gave Mr Cowdell a key and 33 6d for the summons. On going to the house. Mr Cowdell found that the defendant was still living in the house and that the door was locked with the key inside. The key which had been given to Mr Cowdell was not the proper one. Mr Cowdell returned the money to her and she used more abusive langu age.—Thomas Cowdell deposed"that he was wearing a new snit of clothes when the defendant threw the soap suds over him. When the defendant paid the cost ofthe summons and brought him alkey he agreed not to proceed with the case,but on visiting the house he found papers across the windows but the defendant was in possession of the house with the door locked. She was having a hearty breakfast and had not given him the right key —The Mayor thought Mr Cowdell had compromised himself by accepting the cost of the summons. —Mr Fowler sal i the defendant did not carry out her part of the agreement as she had not given tip the proper key:— The defendant said she sold a pair of bedsteads in order to Pay Mr Cowdell the 3s 6d which he afterwards returned to nor. She was unable to get out of the house in time. There were two keys to the house and the one given to Mr Cowdell would have opened the door had not the other key been in. —The magistrates ordered her to pay the costs 4s 6d. The defendant said she had only 4s whereupon the magistrates reduced the order to 4s. ON THE WAY To THE PAWN BHOP.—Miebael McHugh. 87 PierPoint-street,was summoned at the instance of Hannah Young, 94 Pierpoint-street, on a charge of assault.—The compialnant's Story WAS that On the 13th inst, the detenix4s

wife asked her to pawn a shawl for her at Bank Quay. She was met on the way by defendant who asked her for the shawl and struck her on the breast, face and head.—The defendant said the complainant was in the habit of taking articles to the pawn shop for his wife and vt drink for doing so.—The Mayor (to complainant) Are you in the habit of taking things for people to the pawn shop 7—Complainant ; Yes Igo when I am asked.—Are you the woman in that neighbourhood who generally does this thing for neighbours? —I go for about three people,—The Mayor. Do you make a business of it? No.—The Mayor: But you get money for doing it?—Complainant: I sometimes get lid.—The magis- trates decided to dismiss the case. WOMEN 8 QUARBELS —Mary Lawrence of 181. Winwick- road was summoned on a charge of assaulting Agnes Lloyd, of 118 Winwick-road. A cross summons had been taken out by Lawrence charging Lloyd with assault.—Mrs Lloyd, who appeared in Court with two black eyes, stated that on the 20th inst,l Mrs Lawrence came across to her bouse and '• beat her right well 'giving her two black eyes and other- wise assaulting her.—Mrs Morris, a neighbour, stated that Mrs Lawrence terrorised the neighbourhood, A daughter of Mrs Lloyd spoke to the assault on her mother.—Mrs Lawrence admitted the assault but stated that she had received great provocation. The !trouble arose because she would not go drinking with Mrs Lloyd and neighbours, They were always fuddling and drinking, and she would not have anything to do with them. On the day in question Mrs Lloyd struck her and she retaliated. She admitted giving Mrs Lloyd a rood thrashing.- Edith Lawrence having given evidenCe,stbe magistrate ordered each party to pay a tine of , lOs including costs. A. Woatex's Mulcrone. of Turner-street was summoned at the Instance of Emma Jane Bayles of 36 Turner-street on a charge of using threats on Sunday. the 21st inst. As the result of a quarrel, the complapant stated that•the defendant came to her with a knife up .ioor sleeve and threatened to "put it in her heart." Witness was afraid of her.—Mrs Sutton. a neighbour, gave evidence and ' the defendant was ordered to be hound over to keep the peace for six months and pay the costs eta; en shillings.

A Womeresi VlOLENCE.—Elizabeth Dolan. was charged with committing a breach of the peace, by being disorderly In Winwickestreet. at one o'clock that morning and also with breaking four panes of glass at the dwelling house of William Giles, 32, Golden Grove-street.—P C Dyson stated that at the time in question, whilst on duty in Winwiek- street, he heard someone causing a great disturbance near the Central Station. He proceeded there and found the prisoner in a very excited condition, and with a boot in her hand. She said she had smashed some windows, and at his request she took him to Golden Grove-street, I where he saw that four panes of glass had been broken- When she was locked up she said she would smash some more windows when she came out.—William Giles, 32. Golden Grove-street, said that at about one o'clock that morning he was in bed, and was awakened by someone knocking at the door. He looked out of the window and saw the prisoner who asked him to let her in. He refused, and said that if she did not go away he would send for a policeman. She then pulled her shoe off and smashed the windows. Prisoner was a perfect stranger to him, and he had never seen her before. The four panes of glass were worth about 2s.—Prisoner was fined 10s and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment.
