THE THORN INN APomorON.—Mrs Ann Britoil, applied through Kr Crompton (Browne and Crompton. Warrington) for temporary authority to sell, as executrix under the will of her late husband (Mr James Britch), who died recently. at the Thom Inn. Appleton.—The application was granted, A Youxo MAN'S DISGRACEFUL CONDUCT.—Jobn Picker- ing, a young man, was charged with having on the 29th, June, at Little Leigh, assaulted Jessie Withenshaw, married woman. Mr Forshaw appeared for the defendant. —The complainant, who fainted as soon as she had given her evidence, said the defendant was a servant employed by her husband and lived with them in the house. He was paid so much a week. About two o'clock on the morning in question he came into her bedroom and turned up the clothes. This awoke her, and when she looked up she was terrified. He said to her" Let me come." She replied "If you don't clear away I will make your face to that you won't know It." She ordered him out of the room and he went. She got out of bed and fastened the door. She must then have fainted because when she awoke she found her- self lying on the floor. Later on, at about five o'clock, the defendant came to the outside of the door and asked her to forgive him. She replied " No, you had better take yin!f things and go away. ' She was the mother of three children, and or e of them was In the bed with her at the time of the assault. Her husband kept a small farm but was in the employ of Brunner, Mond and Company, and on the night in question he was at work on a " night shift."—ln answer to Mr Forshaw, complainant said that the defendant had lived with them on the farm for about 15 months and up to the present occasion bad behaved himself properly.—David Wlthinshaw said that the com- plainant was his wife, and when he returned home on the morning of the 30th June, his wife complained to him of the assault. She then fainted. The story she then told him was exactly the same as that she had just told to the Bench. she had not been well since, and had been unable to go through her work as usual—By Mr Forshaw : He did not thrash the defendant when he heard his wlfe's story; in fact. ' defendant was not to be seen. Later in the day he saw him and asked him to leave, but as defendant refused to do so he threw him out of the house. Ile considered defendant's conduct was " abominable In any civilised world," —At this stage of the proceedings Mr Forshaw on behalf of his client said he wanted to express his deep regret that the assault had been committed. The fact was defendant Was half asleep and went Into the bedroom in mistake. He denied absolutely having assaalted the complainant.—Mr Within- shaw (in surprise) : Half asleep and asking deliberately to be allowed 'to go into the bed. A man cannot he asleep when be acts in such a manner as that.—The Clerk (to Mr Withinshaw) : You don't wish to press the case do you?— Mr Withinshaw : Not if the defendant will make a public apology and pay all the costs.—Mr Forshaw again expressed regret at the occurrence, and repeated that toe defendant went to the bedroom in mistake and left the moment he was I requested to do so.—The case was then dismissed on payment I of the costs.

div.head: CHESHIRE CHIEF SUPERINTEN-
div.p: CHESHIRE CHIEF SUPERINTEN-
DENT'S RETIREMENT.
Served in the Warrington Force

With the close of the month of July, Mr. Nathan Large, Chief Superintendent of Police of the County of , Chester, and Superintendent of the division of North-1 wich add Middlewich, brings to a close 29 years' honour- able conne tion with the force of the cheese county. I Althotaela he is but 52 years of age and is retiring on al pension by reason of ill-health, his life has been full of incident, and has been a record of successful service- A member of an old Cheshire family, he was quite a boy when he started life as a soldier in the Royal Garrison Artillery. After three years he became a constable in the Warrington Borough force. At the age of 20, he transferred to the Cheshire County Con- stabulary. Serving at Hyde, at Farndon, and Tarporley, he was brought into prominence by his detection of the "hunting gentleman frauds," a mysterious burglary, and a number of other crimes. He was soon promoted to the rank of sergeant, and in 1880 be became full in- spector. and five years later superintendent of the Mac- clesfield division.

He undertook some of the most difficult work in the Cheshire force, and, as superintendent of the Runcorn division during the construction of the Manchester Ship Canal, he had charge of 13 miles of country in which shebeening and other lawlessness was rife. He was suc- cessful here as elsewhere, and his reward came by the transference to Middlewich in 1899 and in May of this year by his appointment as Chief Superintendent of Cheshire.

The Standing Joint Committee of the county, every lonich of magistrates with which he has been associated and many public bodies, have paid tribute to his worth and to the loss the county is sustaining by his retire- ment. Public presentations are being arranged.

NORTHERN UNION FOOTBALL. Financial Difficulty at Runcorn. The Runcorn Club is experiencing some difficulty with its players, as only Roughten,the captain, has signed on, the others, so far,having refused to sign. The diffi- culty is a financial one,the players contending that they were promised one-third of the gate of Batley Cup Tie last season, and this has not lmen paid. The committee contend the money was contingent on the team winning. Yorkshire Senior Competition. Strange Proceedings.

At a meeting of the Yorkshire Senior Competition held on Tuesday night at Leeds it was resolved to leave Hull Kingston Rovers out of the Competition next season. This action is due, it is understood, to the refusal of the Rovers to join in the " boycott " of the Northern League tlubs agreed upon by the Senior Com- petition clubs live weeks ago. By so doing the Rovers would lose their valuable fixture wi h Hull, but as Kingston 'have already been refused admission to the Northern League, they are now in a most awkward pre- dicament.. Dewsbury, Heckmondwike, Keighley,Goole, Normanton, and Sowerby Bridge were admitted to the Competition in place of clubs which have joined the Northern League. Lancashire Business.

The annual 'general meeting of the Lancashire Senior Competition was held on 'Tuesday even- ing at the Spread Eagle Hotel, Manchester. Mr J H Houghton, the president occupied the chair. The balanc”-sheet which showed the useful sum in hand of £231 13111 d on a turnover:of 2799 13s 4d.,was unanimously adopted. The following gentlemen were elected members of the committee ; Messrs B Ashton (Werneth). J H Mills (Abbey. Hills), R Walmsley (Sal- ford), J Parker (Barrow), T Wilkinson (Lancaster), W J Dance (Morecambe), and T Worthington (Swinton). The Junior Cup Rule 11 was altered to read as follows : —MI clubs shall be required to send to their opponents, at least ten days before each tie, a list of bona fide playing members,"and from:such list only shall teams be made up. No player shall play for more than one club in the same season's cup-ties. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the president for his services during his year of office. The following officials were elected for the ensuing season, viz : President, R Collinge (Rochdale Hornets); vice-presideett, R Walmsley, (Salford) ; bon treasurer, E Gresty (Broughton Rangers) •, tion secretary, J Platt (Oldham). Messrs J Tyrer (St Helens) and J W Soholes were re-elected auditors. The selection of venues for the respective county matches was deferred until the fourteenth of August. South. East Lancashire Competition Bye-Laws. The following important bye-laws in connection with the South-East Lancashire Competition were passed at a meeting held at the Spread Eagle Hotel, Manchester, on Tuesday evening :- I.—That the competition be called the South-East Lancashire Rugby Competition. 2.—That an entrance fee of £3 3s he charged, with an annual subscription of £4 4s, the same to be paid before November 1 in each year, 3.—That the management be vested in the Lanes- shire County Committee, and that the competition be subject to the bye-laws of the Northern League so far is applicable. 4.—That each club be compelled to play its best available team in competition matches, and clubs fail- ineito do so be liable to a penalty of £25 for each offence. s.—That a cup be provided, to be held by the winners of the competition during the following season, and 15 gold medals, of the value of £1 10s each, shall be pre- sented to the winning team. 6.—That the referees fee be £1 is to Northern League clubs and 1s 6d to Lancashire Senior Competition clubs; touch-judges to receive 7s fld and 5s respectively; third class railway fares to be added in each came. 7.—Players upon the registers of the Northern League or Lancashire Senior Competition shall be eligible to play for their respective clubs in this competition. B.—The bottom club of the competition at the end of each season shall retire, but shall be eligible for re election.

The Pony and the Motor Car. About two o'clock on Monday afternoon, a pony, attached to a governess ear, belonging to Mr It A Naylor, Cuerden Hall, Tbelwall, was standing in Sankey-street, near to Mr Southerden's (jeweller's) shop. when a motor car belonging to Messrs C and A Husker, engineers, Tuebrook, Liverpool, was pro- ceeding along Sankey-street in the direction of Manchester. The pony became restive and shied, 'backing the governess cs,r into the motor, causing the latter vehicle to be Jammed against the curb- stone. Fortunately the motor car was only travel- ling at a slow pace, but both the wheels of the governess car were broken,and the lamp on the off- . side of the motor car was damaged.

The C.E.T.S.

- . On Thursday, Friday and Saturday the Secretary and seven members of the staff of the Liverpool Diocesan C.E.T.S. assisted by eight ladies, attended the Show of the Royal Lancashire Agricultural Society at Grange Park, St Helens. The C.E.T.S. Marquee 45 feet by 30 feet was erected and about four bundred gallons of drinks suitable for use in farm work were prepared and distributed free in sample glasses together with about 30,000 copies of recipes and other literature. It is estimated that about eight thousand persons availed them- selves of the opportunity of tasting the drinks. On the second evening upwards of 200 grooms, herdsmen &T., attending the show with their employers stock, were provided with a supper. An entertainment provided by members of the Society's Staff was subsequently held and presided over by the Mayor of St Helens, Alderman John Forster, J.P.

div.head: WARRINGTON CORPORATION STOCK. How It Can be Raised. Rejoinder 1;177:-Bugy Bee."
div.p: WARRINGTON CORPORA- TION STOCK. How It Can be Raised. Rejoinder 1;177:-Bugy Bee."

Last week under the heading of " The Question of Corporation Finance" we published a reply to some remarks of our correspondent " Busy Bee."* By a printer's error the name of Alderman Shaw- Green, Chairman of the Finance Committee, was omitted from the reply, in which, it will be remem- bered, "Busy Bee " was asked to reply to six ques- tions bearing upon the subject of the creation of Warrington Corporation stock. This week our reporter called upon" Busy Bee" and asked him if he had any rejoinder to make to Alderman Shaw Green's interrogations. "Yes," he said, "I am glad to exchange views with Alderman Shaw Green on the subject. It is not the first time we have discussed this subject of municipal finance in your columns, for so far back as 18,1 we debated the point. Many of the sugges- tions which I made in the articles at that time have since been carried out. Some of them were declared impossible and others Utopian, but I am glad to say we have made some progress since then, and I am quite willing to give the Corporation credit for what they have done. We have now got the assessments of the borough at the figure I contended they ought to have been some years ago; I' re are now favoured with a municipal balance sheet (about which I shall have something to say presently);lwe havegot an electric light installation and in a very short time we shall have municipal trams. I am anxious that the Corporation should not fritter away its in- creased revenue on things which can well wait for pressing necessities. First and foremost amongst the necessities of Warrington is the provision of a single span bridge in place of the present one across theiMersey,of not leas than 60 feet in width. I went into that subject:a fortnight ago and in suggesting a ways and means of providing the money without increasing the rates, I referred to the saving it was possible for the Finance Committee to effect by the creation of Corporation stock instead of advertis- ing every week for loans. It is this part of my communication to which Alderman Green refers and asks for information. I am glad that he re- cognises the sincerity of my motives and I shall be very pleased to reply, as fully as possible, to his questions. "In the first place let me say a word or two on the subject of Corporation stock itself. It is quite a new institution. In the year 1880, the constantly increasing success which had attended the bringing out of the Metropolitan Consolidated Stock, through the medium of the Bank of England, induced the corporations of Bir- mingham, Liverpool and Nottingham to take steps for obtaining similar powers to those contained in the Loans Act,of the Metropolitan Board of Works, for the purpose of enabling them to convert the whole of their existing loans into stock, charged indifferently on all the rates leviable by,and all the funds and revenues belonging:to them, and for the further purpose of enabling them to raise their future loans by the issue of the same stock. The necessary powers for these purposes were obtained by means of local acts. In the session of 1881,1ocal acts were obtained for the same purposes by the corporations of Birkenhead, Hull, Reading, Scaly- bridge and Swansea. In the following session, similar powers were obtained by the corporations of Blackburn, Bolton, Derby, Halifax, Huddersfield, Macclesfield, Newcastle-upon-Tyne, Rotherham, Tynemouth and Wolverhampton. Since then many other authorities have obtained similar powers, as you will see by looking over a list of Corporation stocks. "Now then, if it has been found so beneficial to the towns referred to, why not Warrington ? I may say in passing that I have appeared bsfore a House of Commons Committee in support of one of these applications for power to create Corporation stock so that 1 claim to know something of the subject. Powers would have to be obtained by an Act to be intituled, "The Warrington Corporation Act, 1901 relating to Corporation stock." With regard to existing securities it would be necessary to ob- tain a section similar to the following which has been granted to a local municipal authority, viz "Where any mortgage, bond, debenture, deben- ture stock, annuity, rent-charge, or other statutory security, granted or created before or after the passing of this Act, by the Corporation under any statutory borrowing power, or other power, is out- standing or payable and the Corporation have power with the consent of the holder of that statutory security, OR OTHERWISE to pay off the amount thereby secured, or represented, or to redeem the same, they may pay off, or redeem the statutory security accordingly with money raised by corporation stock, or they may with the consent of the holder thereof, issue Corporation stock in substitution for the statutory security. The corporation may create and issue corporation stock to such amount as ima3 be requisite for purposes of this section, and that stock shall be deemed to be created and issued, and any money raised thereby, shall be deemed to be raised by virtue of the statutory borrowing power, or other power, under which the statutory security was granted or created, and any money so raised, shall be applied in payment off or redemption of the statutory security, In every such case of payment off, redemption, or substitution the corporation shall pay, and transfer into the loans fund,the whole, or a propor- tionate part (as the case may require) of any•money and securities forming part of any sinking fund applicable to the discharge of the statutory security. 'Where the holder Atha statutory security is one of the persons described in section seven of Lands Clauses Consolidation Act, 1815, and by that Act enabled to sell land thereunder, that person may consent to payment, or redemption of or substitu- tion for the money secured, or represented by that security, and may accept money for giving that consent as if the person so consenting were the absolute owner of that security, and that person is hereby indemnified for so doing, and his receipt shall be a good discharge for the same. Money received by the bolder of any statutory security as authorized by this section, and corpora- tion stock issued to him in substitution for any statutory security, shall be subject to the same trust, powers, testamentary and other dispositions, provisions,and incumbrances, as the money secured or represented by the statutory security, was sub- ject to immediately before the payment off,redemp- tion, or substitution, and every testamentary or other disposition, shall take effect with reference to the whole, or a proportionate part of the money or stock received or substituted,as the caselmay be.' "Having obtained the Act, let us see what the effect would be. If you turn to the balance sheet of the Corporation, for the year ending 31st March last, you will find that the liabilities of Warrington Corporation are stated to be £858,029, and the assets £1,183,850. Alderman Green sake me to work out .the cost of an issue of stock of the nominal amount of .ClOO,OOO. If stock is to be created at all by the Warrington Corporation, a much larger sum than that must be applied for. Let us go in for the whole thing. In 1894, Alderman Green admitted that the interest paid by the Corporation on loans averaged about £3 5s per cent. I should not be sur- prised if it were more than that now. The towns I have referred to borrow at 3 per cent and their stock fluctuates between 98 to 101. There is no reason why Warrington could not do the -same, especially as the Corporation has better security in relation to surplus assets over liabilities. I reckon that the annual amount at present paid by the Warrington Corpor- ation for interest and sinking fund amounts in the aggregate to £43,575. The amount payable under the proposed method of Corporation stock would be £37,350, shewing a saving of £6,225. I am great- ly handicapped in drawing any comparison between the two methods in consequence of the lack of a profit and loss account. Why cannot we have in addition to a Corporation balance sheet a profit and loss account? On the revenue side we could then have the amount received from rates, and the receipts and profits derived from various under- takings. On the other side of the account we want to see what the amount paid in interest and sink- ing fund really totals up to,together with the other expenditure on the different rate funds. Such a statement would be far more intelligible than the present abstract of accounts. "But to return to Mr Alderman Green's first ques- tion. lie asks for a great deal of detail information bearing on the cost of the issue of stock. Much depends on the amount issued and the bank which takes the matter in hand. The Birmingham, Hull, Liverpool, Nottingham and Swansea Corporation itocks have been brought out under the management of the Bank of England. The Reading Corporation stock

was brought out by the London and Westminster Bank, With that spirit of reciprocity which exists between Corporations I have no doubt the Finance Committee will be able to obtain information at first hand from Corporations who have done what I am now advocating. I daresay the Corporation bankers—the Manchester and Liverpool District Banking Company—would take the matter in hand for the Corporation. It is quite an easy matter for the Corporation to call in an expert who has an inti- mate knowledge of this work, and ask him to pre- pare a report on the whole matter as it would affect Warrington. The Finance Committee may be sure of this that other Corporations who have crea- ted stock have been in quite as good a position as the Warrington Corporation, if not better, for negotiating loans, and it must have been to their advantage to create stock, or they would not have got an Act for the purpose. An important matter which ought to be taken into consideration in con- nection with this stock is the fact that the periods prescribed for thedepayment of by far the larger amount of the moffeys authorised to be borrowed by local authorities, under the local Acts of 1881, are considerably in excess of sixty years, which is the longest period allowed for the repayment of loans raised under the general law, and that the repay- ment in some cases has been allowed to extend over 100 years or upwards. The mere fact that the Warrington Corporation after an existence of a little over 50 years, can show an excess of assets over liabilities amounting to £300,000 proves, I think, that the present generation is being called upon to pay more than its fair share for permanent improvements. "My reply to question number two is that money cannot be borrowed upon mortgage as cheaply as by the issue of stock. "With reference to my statement that the cost of the new bridge could be paid out of the saving effected by the issue of stock, I may put it in this way. The bridge costs say £20,000 repayable at 3 per cent. interest on loan and 1i per cent. sinking fund. That would mean £9OO per annum. I have shown a.saving of £6,225 per annum. _ _ .

"Coming to the fourth question, I do not think the town has yet received the finest effott of the Chairman and members of the Finance Committee and the Borough Treasurer, and the public of War- ington, I believe, are waiting to give them that great round of applause that will follow this effort I have alluded to. - -
"Dealing with the fifth question, I would say to the Finance Committee, see to it that no important work is commenced until the borrowing of the money is sanctioned and raised by the issue of stock.

The last question deals with my statement that the Corporation had borrowed £120,000 of the bank at 4 per cent upon it. On referring to the Muni- cipal Balance Sheet I find it there statad that the amount owing to the bank is £124,165. If che rate of interest does not now run up to 4i per cent will Alderman Shaw Green tell us what rate of in- terest has been paid and how much higher than the £3 5s be said the Corporation were borrowing money at i* 1894?
*For the convenience of our country readers we have re- produced Alderman Shaw Green's letter on page 7.

div.head: NEW CONSTABULARY
div.p: THE NEW CONSTABULARY
BUILDINGS.

Date of Opening, The erection of the new constabuiary buildings in Arpley-street, is being rapidly proceeded with. Mr Davenport has made such good progress with the work that the architects felt justified in reporting to the Watch Committee that the magisterial portion of the buildings would be ready for use early in October. At the meeting of the committee last week it was decided to open the magisterial portion on the 11th of October. His Worship the Mayor has been invited to perform the ceremony. It may be stated that the Court Room is almost completed. It is a commodious and well lighted room and a great improvement upon the present stuffy room in Irlam-street which serves for a police court. The officers quarters which are to be provided in con- nection with the new building will be ready at a later date.

div.p: THE EXAMINER FRIDAY, AUGUST 2, 1901:

div.head: SERIOUS FIRE AT THE CABLE WORKS.
div.p: SERIOUS FIRE AT THE CABLE WORKS.
Two Men Injured.

A lire of considerable dimenr-ions occurred on I Friday at the works of the St Helens Cable Company Limited, electrical cable and rubber manufacturers, Bank Quay. The outbreak occurred about 5-30 in one of the departments where the process of braid- rig and lead-covering the cables is chiefly carried oa. At one end of this room are four large tanks containing a solution of " Compo " into which toe cables are stee-ded. The admix- ture contains inflammable material, one of its constituents being naphtha. Two explana- tions have been made as to the cause of the fire. One is that an electric wire fused and a spark fell into a naphtha tank. The other explanation is that two men were engaged in wheeling a can of naphtha, which they bad brought from another part of toe works, when it suddenly tilted and the inflammable liquid falling upon some hot steam pipes immediately burst into flame. A labourer who was passing at the time was caught by the flame and seriously t ..it about the face, arms and neck. He was conveyed to the Infirmary in a cab and it was ascertained that his name is Peter Walsh, 39 yeas of age, of King-street. At the time of the, outbreak this room was filled with work-people, including a number of girls who were working at the machines. An alarm was given and terror-stricken, they rushed out of the works. Meanwhile the naphtha flame had reached the tanks already mentioned and filled the building with a dazzlinc, light. Constructed for the most part-of timber the rafters fell an easy prey to the flames, and as the beams were as dry as tinder, the roof was soon ablaze. The Warrington Fire Brigrde had been tele- phoned for and when they arrived on the scene withthe lire engine "Captain" the roof was crackling and sending forth a dense:cloud of smoke. At the outset Superintendent Turner and his men as well as the fire brigade from Messrs Crosfield's works with a manual engine, endeavoured to make use of the river water, but this was found unsuit- able, and it was wisely decided to discard it in favour of the large reservoir of water belonging to the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company which was in close pro....imity. Fortunately at the time there was little or no wind and the tire did not spread to the adjoining buildings A plentiful supply of water having now been obtained the firemen worked incessantly and poured a volume of water on the burning building with telling effect. The firemen were reinforced by a 5ec0...4 portion of the Warrington Brigado,whd came with the fire engi-e "Major,""and who were supplemen- ted a little ater by the Wilderspool Brigade with the steam engine "Empress". With three engines at work the firemen obtained a complete mastery of the flames, but not before the roof had been des- troyed. At intervals portions of it fell with a crash on the machinery and tanks below. The firemen stuck manfully to their work, and at length they had the satisfaction of knowing they had overcome the flames. The ruins continued to smoulder,but the constant stream of water completely removed all danger. The adjoining buildings were in no way damaged but the large building in which the fire occurred sustained damage to the extent of several thousands of pounds, s ome expensive machinery being damaged by the falling roof and water. The damage is covered by insurance. A fall of glass inflicted a cut on th 3 hand of a workman named John Connor, whose injuries were attended to at the infirmary.

div.head: QUESTION OF CORPORATION FINANCE.
div.p: THE QUESTION OF COR- PORATION FINANCE.

A Reply to "Busy Bee." I am sure your correspondent "Busy Bee" must be very grateful to you for the many opportunities you have afforded him to air his special idea of municipal finance. The financial part of his com- munication, of Saturday last is not new and really does not deserve notice but I recognise the sincerity of his motives and I would like him to give us some clear detail of his views so that we may be able to realize the accuracy or otherwise of his opinion. I venture therefore to ask him to consider and reply to the following questions. I.—Will he work out the cost of an iF.Sue of stock say of the nominal amount of £lOO,OOO with all its incidental charges of issuing—Bank charges, post of investing the sinking fund, increased cost of manipulation &c., as com- pared with borrowing the same sum upon . mortgage with all possible cost of charges for an equal period? 2.—ls he of opinion that money cannot be bor- rowed upon mortgage as cheaply i.e„ at as low a rate as such money can be obtained upon an issue of stock? 3.—Will he be so good as to show us by figures the evidence upon which he bases his state- , ment that the cost of a new bridge over the Mersey could be obtained out of the differ- ence between an issue of stock and the pre- sent method of borrowing upon mortgage. 4.—ls he of opinion that the treasurer, the chairman and members of the Finance Com- mittee are not doing their utmost to ease the burdens upon the ratepayers by financing as cheaply as possible ?-11 he does think so will he kindly show us a better way and prove it. s.—Mr Busy Bee perhaps does not know that money may only be borrowed after authority has-been obtained. May I enquire how he would act if he could not obtain temporary assh•tance from the Bank. 6.—Will he kindly give us the evidence be has in support of his statement that the Corporation ' were owing to the Bank £120,000 and paying, 4i per cent upon it. J. SHAW GREEN.

div.p: WARRINGTON.

Music in. the Park. Mr T. J Down's military band will play the following selection of music, (weather permitting), on Thursday evening, commencing at 7 o'clock. Conductor: Mr T J Down, propramme, 1, March, " Unter dem Freibeitsbanner," Nowowiesky ; 2, overture, " Lestocq," Auber ; 3 raise, " Liebes- trilume," Ertl ; 4, selection, "A Gaiety Girl," Jones; 5, Polka, " Bon Jour," Andrew ; 6, fantasia, " Re- miniscences of England," Godfrey ; 7, hymn, " Eventide," Monk; "God Save the King." Interesting Wedding at the Parish Church,-- Charlesworth—Lewis. A large congregation assembled in the Warring- ton Parish Church on Monday afternoon to witness the solemn:ration of the marriage of Mr Isaac Chariesworth, formerly of Worksov, but for some years resident in Warrington, and Miss Elizabeth (Cisoie) Lewis. eldest daughter of Mr and Mrs Robert Lewis, Upper Bank-street. The bride,dressed in white silk, with a white toque, and Carrying a shower bouquet of white roses and lilies of the valley and also weving a gold brooch, the gift of ' the bridegroom, was conducted to the altar by her father, and was attended by two of her sisters, the ' Misses Edith and Emily Lewis,as bridesmaids. They were attired in flowered muslin, and each wore a gold brooch, the gift of the bridegrootn,They carried shower bouquets of cornflowers and sweet peas also the gifts of the bridegroom. The bride's present to the bridegroom was a gold locket. Mr W E Ingram officiat6d as" best man." The service was conduct- ed by the Rev A S Cameron.- The bridal party and guests afterwards re-assemoled at the home of the bride's parents, where the usual festivities took place. The toast of " Health, prosperity and happi- ness to Mr and Mrs Charlesworth" was proposed by an old friend of the family.and met with the hearti- est response. The presents numbered over 50, and were all of a useful as well as ornate character, some of them being very valuable. Amongst them were a pair of gold-lined silver salts and spoons in case " with affection and esteem from the teachers and scholars of St Clement's Mission," connected with which institution both bride and bridgroom are very earnest workers.

div.p: LATEST NEWS.
Death of the War Minister's
Wife.

Lady Hilda Brodrick. wife of the Secretary of State for War, died early on Thursday morning. Death was due to acute blood-poisoning, for which she was attended by Sir Felix Semen and Dr Manley Sims. Lady Hilda, who was married to Mr Broderick in 1330, was a daughter of the ninth Earl of Wemyss and March. The deceased lady leaves ORO son and four daughters.

div.head: WAR.
div.p: THE WAR.
LATEST TELEGRAMS.
Boers Invade Portuguese Territory.
Opposed by Portuguese Troops.
LOURENC3 MAIMrES WEDNESDAY.-A Ther com- mando, with two guns,bas crossed into Portuguese territory, and camped at Guanetz.
Five lauadred Portuguese troops are already on the spot.
Artillery left here this morning, and 300 more troops are in readiness to proceed to Guanetz unless the Boers surrender.
MURDER OF NATIVES.
Official Message.
The following was issued by the War Office on Thursday evening : From Lord Kitchener to the Secretary of State for War.
PRETORIA, ArausT 1.
French reports he has received a letter from Kritzinger announcing his intention to shoot all natives in the British employ, whether armed or unarmed.
Many cases of cold-blooded murder of natives in Cape Colony have recently cccurred.
Mishap to Yeomanry.
Native Scouts and Wounded Yeoman Shot.

From Lord Kitchener to the Secretary of State for War. BESIDENCY, PRETORIA, AVSEST 1, 9 25, R.ITI. On the 26tb July an officers' patrol of 20 Yeo- manry and some native acout4 followed two carts and a few Boers to a distance of 15 miles from the railway, at Doom n River, Orange River Colony. They were there cut off by about 200 Boers, and after defending themselves in a small building sur- rendered, their ammunition being exhausted. Three Yeomen were wounded. After surrender the Boers made native scouts hold up their hands, and shot them in cold blood. Afterwards shot one wounded yeoman, Trooper Finch. Remainder were released. The reason for shooting Finch,the Boers said they 4 thought he was a Cape boy. A board ef enquiry will be held, and evidence on oath taken of the murders.

div.head: Warrington Militia to Arrive To-Day.
div.p: The Warrington Militia to Arrive To-Day.

Colonel Ireland Blackburne, the Commanding Officer of the 31.1 Battalion South Lancashire Regiment (Militia) lass sent home a message to the effect that the Pinemore will arrive at Southampton on Friday, and that the men of the 3rd Battalion (Militia) South Lanca- shire Regiment will travel so as to reach Warrington about seven o'clock on Saturday morning. Arrange- ments have been made to entertain them to breakfast at the Drill Hall, immediately on arrival.

div.head: NOTES BY THE WAY AT . EARLESTOWN.
div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY AT . EARLESTOWN.
[BY A CORRESPONDENT.]
CRICKET.

Earlestown came within an ace of defeating Wigan on the latter's ground on Saturday,as it was they made a draw of it, favourable to themselves. The visitors compiled 164 ; and out of this number, Miller made 96, not out, by careful and excellent cricket. Mitchell, the ex-wicket keeper, who has not played this season, was requisitioned to fill a gap, and very useful he proved,making '2O before he was dismissed. Wigan went to the wickets, but only seven of their wickets were accounted for, with 79 runs to their credit. It wnuld have been more satisfactory if Earlestown had won, seeing that they cut such a sorry figure against Wigan a few weeks ago.

The second teams met at Earlestown, but the home eleven never made a poorer show than they did on Saturday. They only managed to put in 55 and four ot the eleven were out for dunks, Greenall and Harrison alone entering double figures. The Wigan team played havoc with the Earlestown bowling, and put on the respectable score of 160 be fore they were dismissed.

div.head: N.S.P.C.C. LEAGUE OF PITY.
div.p: THE N.S.P.C.C. LEAGUE OF PITY.
-- Garden Sale of Work at Stockton Heath.

A work which must commend itself to everyone is that carried on by the National Society for the Preven- tion of Cruelty to Children, and not the least useful department of this philanthropic institution is the Chil- dren's League of Pity. Its object, as briefly stated by the founders, is" to enlist the happy zhildren of the land in the setvice of the unhappy," and it is open to boys and girls under sixteen years of age. It is pleasing to know that a branch of the League is actively carrying on its work in Warrington, Miss Broadbent being the energetic secretary. Evidence of the interest taken in the c,perations of the society by the young people was afforded on Wednesday afternoon when a garden sale of work promoted by the League in aid of the funds of the N.S:P.C.C. was held in the grounds of Heatherdeze, Grappenhall-road, Stockton Heath, the residence of Mr F R Pierpoint. A large number of the articles on sale had been made by the children in the League. who also lent valuable assis tance at the stalls. Fortunately the atmospherical con- ditions were all that could be desired and there was a good attendance at the opening of the sale The stalls were very tastefully arranged in the garden, and were heavily laden with useful and fancy articles, flowers Sic. The following were the stallholders t—Flower stall, Misses Maijory Broadbent, E Roberts, N Longbottom and D Ashley ; sweet stalls, Misses N Wright, L Birtles, and A Burgess ; toy stall Misses C Walker, M Henshall, and C Johnson ; work stall, Miss Broadbent, Mrs Venn, Misses M Perris, S Tongue, and M Randle. There was a fish pond in charge of Misses Pierpoint and Venn, whilst gramaphone en- tertainments were given under the direction of Mr Frank Bickford. Madame Zuleika, palmist, held consultations in a tent. The sale was opened by Mrs Bush, a lady who delivers addresses at various functions held in different parts of the country on behalf of the funds of the Society. She gave some interesting details with regard to the noble work carried on by the N.S.P.C.C. and described the methods adopted, which she said were simple and effective. Since the formation of the Society. she said, a great deal of work had been accomplished,but a great deal remained to be done. Amongst those present during the affernoon were the Revs F .E Powell, A N Taylor, EC E. Carleton and W Bracecamp, Mrs Broadbent, Mrs F A Frost, Miss Rimmer, Mrs NV B Roberts, Mrs Baxter, Mrs Willett, Mrs Jackson H limes and Mrs H N Houghton. At four o'clock and 7.30 con- certs were given, most attractive programmes having been arranged. Sono were effectively rendered by Madame Ethel Newcombe (soprano) and Mr Bantock Pierpoint (baritone) who were heartily ap- plauded for their efforts. The programmes also included pianoforte solos by Miss Houghton and Mrs Jackson Holmes, piano duets by Mrs W B Roberts and Mrs Jackson Holmes, cornet solo by Mr R W Pierpoint, and violin solos by Mrs W B Roberts. All the artistes acquitted themselves admirably. A capital ventriloquial entertainment was also well patronized.
Laay Frederick Cavendish at Warrington.

Lady Frederick Cavendish paid her accustomed visit to the mission in Factory-yard, Bank Quay,on Monday. This mission is the Holy Trinity :Branch of the Parochial Mission Women's Association, of Which the Hon. Elizabeth Wilson-Patten is the lady superintendent. Lady Frederick Cavendish is the general manager of all the branches outside of London. Lady Frederick gave a most interesting address to the women, having reference chiefly to the domestic life of our late heloved Queen. The stories and reminiscences she was able to give, many from her own Personal knowledge, were greatly appreciated. The Vicar (the Rev E C E Carleton) was present.

div.head: EXAMINER FRIDAY, AUGUST 2, 1901
div.p: THE EXAMINER FRIDAY, AUGUST 2, 1901
NOTES ON (JAMES AND ATHLETICS.

Cricket. When Warrington met the Cheetham eleven en the latter club's ground, some few weeks ago, the Cheetham contingent secured a victory by the bare nraj,rity of two runs. Last Saturday the return engagement took place at Arpley, and the Warrington team more than fully atoned for their defeat on the former occasion by trouncing the Manchester men to the extent of 79 runs and a wicket to spare. Taking first turn at the wickets, the visitors were all dismissed for the poor total of 64. When play ceased for the day Warrington had compiled 143 for the loss of 9 wickets, J W Bibby, the home captain, not having had the chance of displaying his powers with the bat.

The Warrington captain certainly showed good judg- ment in allowing the visitors to li-‘t first or. a slow wicket, for the pitch improved the match pro- gressed, and Warrington bad au easy task. Both Thewlis and E Gibson were in rare I,,rm with the ball, Gibson in particular miking the ball turn quickly off the pitch, and the balls which dismissed the brothers ISinclair were rare specimens. From the start the bowlers always held the upper ilarid, and alter T Sinclair had torcul the game in compiling his 14. W Parker of the remainder looked like giving trouble, and his innings of 17 was the best contribution on the visit- ing side. A. fine return by W P.odaiore was responsible for the dismissal of Halliday, and the venture closed for 64. E Gibson bowled a splendid length throughout,and his six wickets for 29 runs must rank as one of his most creditable performances this season.

.7 Callon and B Silcock were the first batsmen to represent Warrington, and af'nr the former bad got Parker away twice to the leg boundary and had made 14 out of the 17 chronicled be was bowled by Sinclair. Briggs opened briskly, and the second wicket was responsible for the addition of 16 runs when Briggs was bowled. However, with Thowlis as Silcock's associate a fine stand was made. rho professional batted in superb style, driving both bowlers to the boundary and causing the original bowlers to r,-2tire for Halliday and S Parker.

Runs continued to c-me at a fair pace, and when Thewlis placed Parker for a cluple and the Cheetham score was passed a cneer greeted the performance. Both eontinued their flurry career, and Thewlis soon passed his partner Silcock, who played with his usual char- acteristic patience.

The original bowlers. were again tried, but all to no purpose, whilst with the hoisting of the century Halliday took the ball from Parker, and with his first ball got Thewlis caught at the the 'professional being cheered for a brilliantly hit 44, included in which were six fours. A rzn later Silcock was caught one- handed at point, his 34 beine a model display of pati- ence. Of the other batsmen %V Podmore showed fine form for his 22, being caught on the boundary, and with the home captain not batting the innings closed , for 143.

The sEcond eleven had to bow the knee to Cheetham, 37 being the margin against them. Cheetharn won the toss, and the innings closed for 107. Warrington com- menced their account with C R Adamson and E Pierpoint against the bowling of Maddock and Dippie. With one run on the board Ferguson bowled Pierpoint. Adamson added two more singles, but Allen was unfortunately run out. Crompton was bowled by Dippie with the score at eight. Adamson and Plinston took the score to 38 when Dippie bowled Plinston. The fifth wicket realized 17 when Adamson was bowled by Maddock for a carefully played 14. Fairclough tell a victim to Parker with the same total on the board. All hopes for a victory for Warrington were now overshadowed, as six wickets had fallen for 45 runs. Bradley and Roddy added 20 between them. The innings closed for 70.

div.head: Athletics.
div.p: Athletics.

Sankey Harriers are justly proud .of the success achieved by three of their memiers on Saturday. At the Liverpool Charity Sports,heid on the Stanley ground J A Watson won the half mile bicycle race with a start of 85 yards by two lengths in front of the second man. He was also successful in placing the mile bicycle race to his credit, having received a start of 180 yards. and being a foot ahead of WS nearest competitor. The other two prizes were won at Bell Vue in connection with the Salford Harriers' Sports, 1) Gibson,with an allowance of 20 yards finishing third in the 600 yards obstacle race, whilst E Hilton was fourth in the utile flat race, receiv- ing a start of 113 yards.

Swimming. Oa Tuesday next the Sth inst the Warrington team meet Liverpool City at home. This team is now the best seven in the Liverpool and District League and will include " Bob " Sharracks of County and International fame.

It is to be hoped that the unneccessary ,10a37 caused by the Liverpool teams travelling by the 3.30 train from Liverpool instead of the 7.30 will not occur &vain. To start a match at 9.15 runs the game well on to 10 Velcck and parents necessarily grumble at their youngsterisawho are no mean enthusiasts of the game—being out of bed so late.

On Saturday next the 10th inst the Club holds its annual gala. Trio date is much earlier than in former years and would have been far better could it have been held at the end of next month. The committee were obliged to hold the gala on this date as it is the date fixed by the A. S. A. for the North v Alidland's match, However the ventilation of the bath will be very materially improved for the occasion.

- • The teams in the polo match will include many names well known in the swimming world and many that have appeared at the Corporation Baths, and amongst whom will figure the following :—J H Darbyshire (Man- chester Osborne) 100 yards amateur zhampion and the recognised champion ornamental swimmer—J A Jarvis (Leicester) who will eaptain the Midland team is too well known to need describing. Only so recently as Saturday last Jarvis succeeded in winning the Mersey Championship with the utmost ease. As a polo player he has no superior.—Frank Battersby (Stockport) who recently won outright the Bac'r Stroke Champion, shin. Battersby is considered by all who have seen him to be the finest Cxponent at back and breast stroke swimming of this or any other day. He is billed to give an exhibition in these particular styles and has offered the club the loan of his trophy for public show. "Andy" Robertson, our own townsman, will play in goal for the North. Robertson has on several occasions been selected by the County Executive, and last year played in a sidrilar position for England against ScL•tland. He is a very safe and consistent player.

The Cush have been fortunate in securing the sarvices of Miss Christina Duckworth,of Mancbester,who will give her grand display of scientific and ornamental swimming. Miss Duckworth holds the Lady Amateur Championship for ornamental swimming. She is a pupil of the well- known Mrs Whitehead, of Manchester, who held the Championship for many years previous to her gaining the title by competition. This is a treat which should I not be missed by the gentler at a.

The Championship of the Town and District (Licensed Victuallers Trophy) will figure in the programme as well as the Schoolbdy Championship ( Thornton Chal- lenge Cup). The latter is one of the most popular items of the year and always commends a good entry. There will also be a Club members 50 yards Handicap for valuable prizes.

div.head: MR. J. C. PARR ELECTED AN ALDERMAN.
div.p: MR. J. C. PARR ELECTED AN ALDERMAN.

-- At the quarterly meeting of the Cheshire County Council, held on Thursday morning, at Chester, Mr .1 Charlton Parr was elected an alderman of the county,in the place of the late Alderman J Sykes. Mr Parr has been a member of the Council since its inauguration and has represented the Applet on division during the whole of that time. Prior to the Daresbury Highway Board being absorbed by the Runcorn Rural District Council. Mr Parr was chairman of that body. He I also takes a deep intenst in the Warrington Young Men's Christian Association and his name will long b 0 associated with this town in consequence of his hanisome gift of Parr Hall. Mr Parr was for several years chairman of Parr's Banking Company, bat retired from that position about the time of the amalgamation with the Alliance Bank. Mr Parr's elevation to an aldermanic se: t creates a vacancy in the Appleton (Cheshire) division.

Volunteer Intelligence This week's orders for the ISt Volunteer Battalion (P W V) South Lancashire Regimentannounce that the annual rifle meeting will be held at Altcar on Monday next, the sth August, 1901. A special train will be provided for all duly qualified competitors, who will be given a free ticket. A Competitor to be duly qualified must be efficient in drill and mus- ketry. Non-efficients should arrange to complete their course before the meeting. All entries close at 9 p m to-lay. All competitions will be fired in uniform. Intending competitors will parade at the Drill Hall on Monday next at 8.30 a m, and the battalion thus formed will be marched to the Bank Quay Railway Station for direct conveyance to Altera, returning about 8 pm. The band and bugle band will attend Dress for parade:—Drill order ' (with Kersey frocks) with one pouch, Offir,ro blue merges and putties, without swords. "G" uom- pany will join the battalion at Farleatown station.

div.head: (conright.) A:SHADOW BEFORE.
div.p: (conright.) A:SHADOW BEFORE.
EY A. CONAN DOYLE,
Author of "Micah Clarke," "Adventures of Sherlock Hoboes," "The Stark Munro Letters," "Rodney Stone," "The Exploits of Brivadier Gerard." 3:c.

On July 15th, 1870, John Worlington Dodds was a ruined gamester of the Stock Exchange Upon the 17th he was a very opulent man. And yet he had effected the change without leaving the penurious little Irish townlet of Dunsloe, which could have been bought outright for a quarter of the sum which he had earned during the single day that he was within its walls. There is a romance of finance yet to be written, a story of huge forces which are for ever waxing and waning, of bold operations, of breathless suspense, of agonised failure, of deep combinations which are baffled by others still more subtle. The mighty debts of each great European Power stand like so many columns of mercury, for ever rising and falling to indicate the pressure upon each. He who can see far enough into the future to tell how that ever-varying column will stand to-morrow is the man who has fortune within his grasp. John Worlington Dodds had many of the gifts which lead a speculator to success. He was quick in observing, just in Estimating, prompt and fearless ih acting. But in finance there is always the element or luck Which, however one may elimindte it, still remains, like the blank at roulette, a constantly present handicap upon the operator. And so it was that Worlington Dodds had come to grief. On the best advices he had dabbled in the funds of a South American Republic in the days before South American Republics had been found out. The Republic defaulted and Dodds lost his money. He had bulled the shares of a Scotch railway and a four months' strike had hit him hard. He had helped to underwrite a coffee company in the hope that the public would come along upon the feed and grmivally nibble away some of his holding, but the political sky had been clouded and the public had refused to invest. Everything which he had touched had gone wrong, and now, on the eve of his marriage, young, clear- headed, and energetic, he was actually a bankrupt, had his creditors ^',".sen t=Ake him one But the Stock Exchan is an indulgent bod_y. What is the case of one t• -day may be that o. morrow, and everyone is interest.. in' seeing Agit the stricken man is given tins. to Tise again. So the burden of Worlington Dodd a was lightei4 for him, many shoulders helped to bear it, andjet was able to go for a little summer tour into Ireland, for the doctors had 0n...L:t.3. 1-1.4 to restore his shaken nervous system. Thus it was that ui on July 15th, 1870, he found himself at his bret kfast in the fly-blown coffee-room of the George tiotel in the market square of Dunsloe. It is a dull and depressing coffee-room, and one which is usually empty, but on this particular day it was as crowded and noisy as that of any London hotel. Every table was occupied, and a thick smell of fried bacon and of fish hung in the air. Heavily-booted men clattered in and out, spurs jingled, riding crops were fstacked in corners, and there was a general atmosphere of horse. The con- versation, too, was nothing else. From every side Worlington Dodds heard of yearlings, of wind- galls, of roarers, of spavins, of cribsuckers, of a hundred other terms which were as unintelligible to him as his own Stock Exchange jargon would have been to the company. He asked the waiter for the reason of it all; and the waiter was an astonished man that there should be anyone in this world who did not know it.

"Shure it's the Dunsloe horse fair, your honour —the greatest fair in all Oireland. It lasts for a wake, and the dalers come from far an' near, from England an' Scotland an' iverywhere. If you look out of the. winder, youz'. honour, you'll see the horses, and it's asy your honour's conscience must be or you wouldn't slape so sound that the cratures didn't rouse you with their clatter." Dodds had a recollection that he had heard a confused murmur, which had interwoven itself with his dreams—a sort of steady rhythmic beating and clanking—and now when he looked through the window he saw the cause of it. The square was packed with horses from end to end, greys, bays, browns, blacks, chestnuts, young ones and old, fine ones and coarse, horses of every con- ceivable sort and size. It seemed a huge function for so small a town, and he remarked as much to the waiter.

"Well, you see, your honour, the horses don't live in the town an' they don't vex their heads how small it is. But it's in the very centre of the horse-bradin' districts of Oireland, so where should they come to be sould if it wasn't to Dunsloe ? "

The waiter had a telegram in his hand, and he turned the address to Worlington Dodds. "Shure I niver heard such a name, sorr. Maybe you could tell me who owns it?" Dodds looked at the envelope. Strellenhaus was the name. "No, I don't know," said he. "I never heard it before. It's a foreign name. Perhaps if you were—" . _ _ _

But at that moment a little round-faced, ruddy- cheeked gentleman who was breakfasting at thd next table, leant forward and interrupted him. "Did you say a foreign name, sir ? " said he. " Strellenhaus is. the name."

"I am Mr. Strellenhaus—Mr. Julius Strellen- haus of • Liverpool. I was expecting a telegram. Thank you very much." He sat so near that Dodds, without any wish to play the spy, could not help to some extent over- looking him as he opened the envelope. The message was a very long one. Quite a wad of melon-tinted paper came out from the tawny envelope. Mr. Strellenhaus arranged the sheets methodically upon the table-cloth in front of him, so that no eye but his own could see them. Then he tOok out a note-book, and with an anxious face he began to make entries in it, 'glancing first at the telegram and then at the book, and writing, apparently, one letter or figure at a time. Dodds was interested, for he knew exactly what the man was doing. He was working out a cypher. Dodds had often done it himself. And then suddenly the little man turned very pale, as if the full purport of the thessage had been a shock to him. Dodds had done that also, and his sympathies were all with his neighbour. Then the stranger rose, and, leaving his breakfast untested, he walked out of the room. "I'm thinkin' that the gintleman has had bad news, sort," said the confidential waiter. "Looks like it, Dodds answered, and at that moment his thoughts Were suddenly drawn off into another direction.

The boots had entered the room with a telegram in his hand. • "Where's Mr. Mancune ? " said he to the waiter. "Well, there are spme quare names about. What was it you said? . "Mr. Mancune," said the boots, glancing about him. "Ah, there he is!" and he handed the tele- gram to a gentleman who was sitting reading the paper in a corner. Dodds's eyes had already fallen upon this man, and he had wondered vaguely what he was doing in seh company. He was a tall, white-haired, eagle- nosed gentleman, with a waxed moustache and a carefully pointed beard—an aristocratic type which seemed out of its element among the rough, hearty, noisy dealers who surrounded him. This, then, was i).lr. Mancune, for whom the second telegram , was intended. As he opened it, tearing it open with a feverish haste, Dodds could perceive that it was as bulky as the first one. Ifi observed also from the delay in reading it that it was also in some sort of cypher. The gentleman did not write down any translation of it, but he sat for some time with his nervous, thin fingers twitching amongst the hairs of his white beard, and his shaggy brows bent in the deepest and most absorbed attention whilst he mastered the meaning of it. Then he sprang soddenly to his feet, his eyes flashed, his cheeks flushed, and in his excitement he crumpled the message up in his hand. With an effort he mastered his emotion, put the paper into his pocket, and walked out of tip room. This was enough to excite a less astute and imaginative man than Worlington Dodds. Was there any connection between these two messages, or was it merely a coincidence! Two men with strange names receive two telegrams within a ftw minutes of each other, each of considerable length, each in cypher, and each causing keen emotion to the man who received it. One turned pale. The other sprang excitedly to his feet. It might be a coincidence, but it was a very curious one. If it was not a coincidence, then what could it mean? Were they confederates who uretended to work

apart, but wno eacn received identical orders from some person at a distance! That was possible, and yet there were difficulties in the way. Ile puzzled and puzzled, but could find no satisfactory ablution to the problem. All breakfast he was turning it over in his mind.

When breakfast was over he sauntered out into the market square, where the horse sale was already in progress. The yearlings were being sold first— tall, long-legged, skittish, wild-eyed creatures, who had run free upon the upland pastures, with ragged hair and towsey manes, but hardy, inured to all weathers, and with the makings of splendid hunters and steeplechasers when corn and time had brought them to maturity. They were largely of thoroughbred blood, and were being rought by English dealers who would invest a few pounds now on what they might sell for fifty guineas in a few years if all went well. It was legitimate speculation, for the horse is a delicate creature, he is afflicted with many ailments, the least accident may destroy his value, he is a certain expense and an uncertain profit, and for one who comes safely to maturity several may bring no return at all. So the English horse-dealers took their risks as they bought up the shaggy Irish yearlings. One man with a ruddy face and a yellow overcoat took them by the dozen with as much sang-froid as if they had been oranges, entering each bargain in a bloated note-book. He had bought forty or fifty during the time that Dodds was watching him. "Who is that?" e asked his neighbour, whose spurs and gaiters slimed that he was likely to know. The man stared in astonishment at the stranger's ignorance. "Why, that's Jim Holloway, the great Jim Holloway," said he; then, seeing by the blank look upon Dodds's face that even this information had not helped him very much, he went into details. "Sure he's the head of Holloway and Morland, of London," said he. "He's the buying partmir, and he buys cheap, and the other stays at home and sells, and he sells dear. He owns more horses than any man in the world and asks the best money for them. I daresay you'll find that half of what are gold at the Dunsloe fair this day will go to him, and he's got such a purse that there's not a man can bid against him." Worlington Dodds watched the doings of the great dealer with interest. He had passed on now to the two-year-olds and three-year s, full- grown horses, but still a little .n the limb and weak in the bone. The unckm buyer choosing his animals carefm . but having chosen them the vigour of his compe. ion .drove all other bidders out. of it. With a careless nod he would run the figure up live pounds at a time, unti. Le was left ia possession of the field.: At the same V.sa4-44, "Qs a .1.-krewd observer, anl when, s hap- "pened inore-than 0r... he -leiteviid that someone was bidding agaMet hitt-Ittirti,/in order to run him up, the head would cease itidakly to nod, the note-bock would he closed with a snap, and the intruder would Le left with a puroilisse which he 'did not desire upon his hands. All Dodds's business instincts were aroused by the tactics of this great operator, and he stood in the crowd watching with the greatest interest all that occurred. It is not to buy young horses, however, that the great dealers come to Ireland, and the real business of the fair commenced when the four and five- year-olds were reached, the full-grown, perfect horses at their prime and ready for any work or any fatigue. Seventy magnificent creatures had been brought down by a single breeder, a comfort- able-looking, keen-eyed, ruddy-cheeked gentleman who stood beside the salesman and whispered cautions and precepts into his ear. "That's Flynn, of liildare," said Dodds's in- forthant. "Jack Flynn has brought down that string of horses, and the other large string over , yonder belongs to Torn Flynn, his brother. The two of them together are the two first breeders in Ireland." A crowd had gathered in front of the horses. By common consent a place had been made for Mr. Holloway, and Dodds could catch a glimpse of his florid face and yellow covert coat in the front rank. He had opened his note-hook and was tapping his teeth reflectively with his pencil as he eyed the horses.

"You'll see a fight now between the first seller and the first buyer in the country," said Dodds's acquaintance. "They are a beautiful string, any- how. I shouldn't be surprised if he didn't average five-and-thirty pound apiece for the lot as they stand."

The salesman had mounted upon a chair, and his keen, clean-shaven face overlooked the crowd. Mr. Jack Flynn's grey whiskers were at his elbow, and Mr. Holloway immediately in front. "You've seen these horses, gentlemen," said the salesman, with a backward sweep of his hand towards the line of tossing heads and streaming manes. "When you know that they are bred by Mr, Jack Flynn, at his place in Kildare, you will have a guarantee of their quality. ' They are the best that Ireland can produce, and in this class of horse the best that Ireland can produce are the best in the world, as every riding man knows well. Hunters or carriage horses all warranted sound and bred from the best stock. There are seventy in Mr. Jack Flynn c string, and he bids me say that if any wholesale dealer would make one bid for the whole lot, to save time, he would have prefer- ence over any purchaser." There was a pause and d'whisper from the crowd in front, with some expressions of discontent. By a single sweep all the small dealers had been put out of it. It was only a long purse which could buy on such a scale as that. The salesman looked round him inquiringly. "Come, Mr. Holloway," said he at last. "You didn't come over here for the sake of the scenery. You may travel the country and not see such another string of horses. Give us a starting bid." The great dealer was still rattling his pencil upon his front teeth. "Well," said he at last., "They are a fine lot of horses, and I won't deny it. They do you credit, Mr. Flynn, I am sure. All the same, I didn't mean to fill a ship at a single bid in this fashion. I like to pick and choose my horses." "In that case Mr. Flynn is quite prepared to sell them in smaller lots," said the salesman. "It was rather for the convenience of a wholesale customer that he was prepared to put them all up together. But if no gentleman wishes to bid—' "Wait a minute," said a voice. "They are very fine horses, these, and I will give you a bid to start you. I will give you twenty pounds each for the string of seventy." There was a rustle as the crowd all swayed their heads to catch a glimpse of the speaker. The sales- man leant forward.

"May I ask your name, sir?" "Strellenhaus—Mr. Strellenhaus, of Liverpool." "It's a new firm," said Dodds's neighbour. "I thought I knew them all, but I never heard of him before." The salesman's head had disappeared, for he waa whispering with the breeder. Now he suddenly straightened himself again. "Thank you for giving us a lead, sir," said he. ."Now, gentlemen, you have heard the offer of Mr. Strellenhaus, of Liverpool. It will give us a base to, start from. Mr. Strellenhaus has offered twenty pounds a head."

"Giiiiieas," said Holloway." "Bravo, Mr. Holloway, I knew that you would take a hand. You are not the man to let such a string of horses pass away from you. The bid is twenty guineas a head." "Twenty-five pounds," said Mr. Strellenhaus. "Twenty-six." "Thirty." It was London against Liverpool, and it was the head of the trade against an outsider. Still, the one man had increased his bids by fives and the other only I v ones. Those fives meant determina- tion and also wealth. Holloway had ruled the market so long that the crowd was delighted at finding someone who would stand up to him. "The bid now stands at thirty pounds a head," said the salesman. "The word lies with you, Mr. Holloway." The London dealer was glancing keenly at his unknown opponent, and he was asking himself whether this was a genuine rival, or whether it was a device of some sort—an agent of Flynn's, perhaps—for running up the price. Little Mr. Strellenhaus, the same apple-faced gentleman whom Dodds had noticed in the coffee-room, stood looking at the horses with the sharp, quick glances of a man who knows what be is looking for. "Thirty-one," said Holloway, with the air of man who has gone to his extreme limit. "Thirty-two," said Strellenhaus, promptly. Holloway grew angry at this persistent opposi- tion. His red face flushed redder still. "Thirty-three," he shouted. "Thirty-four," said Strellenhaus. Holloway became thoughtful, and entered a few figures in his note-book. There were seventy horses. He knew that Flynn's stock was always of t ha highest quality. With the hunting season coming on he might rely upon selling them at an average of from forty-five to fifty. Some of them 6'62154 carry a helm-weight and would run to

three figures. On the other hand there was tne feed and keep of them for three months, the danger of the voyage; the chance of. influenza or some of those other complaints which run through an entire ttsWe as meanies go through a nurserj. Deducting all this, it was a question whether at the present price any profit would be left upon the transaction. Every pound that he bid meant seventy out of his pocket. And yet he could not submit to be beaten by this stranger without a struggle. As a business matter it was important to him to be recognised as the head of his profession. He would make one more effort if he sacrificed his profit by doing so. "At the end of your rope, Mr. Holloway ra asked the salesman, with the suspicion of a sneer.

"Thirty-five," cried Holloway gruffly. "Thirty-six," said Strellenhaus. "Then I wish you joy of your bargain," said Holloway. "I don't buy at that price, but I should be glad to sell you some." Mr. Strellenhaus took no notice of the irony. He was still looking critically at the horses. The salesman glanced round him in a perfunctory way. "Thirty-six pounds bid," said he. "Mr. Jack Flynn's lot is going to Mr. Strellenhaus, of Liver- ` pool, at thirty-six pounds a head. "Forty," cried a high, thin, clear voice. A buzz rose from the crowd, and they were all on tiptoe again, trying -to catch a glimpse of this reckless buyer. Being a tall man Dodds could see over the others, and there at the side of Holloway he saw the masterful nose and aristocratic beard of the second stranger in the coffee-room. A sudden personal interest added itself to the scene. He felt that he was on the verge of something—something dimly seen which he could himself turn to account. The two men with strange names, the telegrams, the horses—what was underlying it all? The salesman was all animation again, and Mr. Jack Flynn was sitting up with his white whiskers bristling and his eyes twinkling. It was the best deal he had ever made in his fifty years of experience. "What name, sir?" asked the salesman. Mancune." "Address? " _

"Mr. Mancune, of Glasgow." "Thank you for your bid, sir. Forty pounds a head has been bid by Mr. Mancune, of Glasgow. A.': advance upon forty ? " Forty-one, ' said Strellenhaus. "borty-five," said Mancune. The tactics had changed, and it was the turn of Strelleal.aus now to advance by ones, while his rival sprang up by fives. But the former was as dogged fo ever. "Forty-six," said he. "Fifty," Cried Mancune. It was unheard of. The most that the horses could possibly average at a retail price was as much as these men were willing to pay wholesale. "Two lunatics from Bedlam," whispered the angry Holloway. "If I was Flynn I would see the colour of their money before I went any further."

The same thought had occurred to the salesman. "As a mere matter of business, gentlemen," said he, "it is usual in such cases to put down a small deposit as a guarantee of bona fides. You will understand how I am placed, and that I have not had the pleasure of doing business with either of you 1-Aore." "How much ? " asked Strellenhaus, briefly. "Should we say five hundred?" "Here is &note for a thousand pounds." "And here is another," said Mancune.

"Nothing could be more handsome, gentlemen," said the salesman. "It's a treat to see such a spirited competition. The last bid was fifty pounds a head from Mr. Mancune. The word lies with you, Mr. Strellenhaus." Mr. Tack Flynn whispered something to ths salesman:

"Quite so! Mr. Flynn suggests, gentlemen, that as you are both large buyers, it would, perhaps, be a convenience to you if he was to add the string of Mr. Tom Flynn, which consists of seventy animals of precisely the same quality,' making one hundred and forty in all. Have you any objection, Mr. Mancune ? " "No, sir." "And you, Mr. Strellenhaus ?". "I should prefer it." "Very handsome! Very handsome indeed!" murmured the salesman. "Then I understand, Mr. Mancune, that your offer of fifty pounds a head extends to the whole of these horses ? "

"Yes, sir." A long breath went up from the crowd. Seven thousand pounds at one deal. It was a record for Druasloe. "Any advance, Mr. Strellenhaus ? " "Fifty-one." "Fifty-five." "Fifty-six." " Sixt y. " They could hardly believe their ears. Holloway stood with his mouth open, staring blankly in front of him. The salesman tried hard to look as if such bidding and such prices *ere nothing un- usual. Jack Flynn, of Kildare, smiled benignly .and rubbed his hands together. The crowd likened in dead silence.

"Sixty-one," said Strellenhaus. From the beginning he had stood without a trace of emotion upon his round face, like a little automatic figure which bid by clockwork. His rival was of a more excitable nature. His eyes were shining, and he was for ever twitching at his beard. "Sixty-five," he cried. "Sixty-six." "Seventy." But the clockwork had run down. No answering bid came from Mr. Strellenhaus.
"Seventy bid, sir." Mr. Strellenhaus shrugged his shoulders. "I am buying for another, and I have reached his limit," said he. "If you will permit me to send for instructions—_—" _

"I am afraid, sir, that the sale must proceed." "Then the horses belong to this gentleman." For the Drat time he turned -towards his rival, and their glances crossed like sword blades. "It is possible that I may see the horses again." "I hope so," said Mancune, and his white waxed moustache gave a feline upward bristle. So, with a bow, they separated. Mr. Strellenhaus walked down to the telegraph office, where hia message was delayed because Mr. Worlington Dodds was already at the end of the wires, for after dim guesses and vague conjecture he had suddenly caught a clear view of this coming event which had cast so curious a shadow before it in this little Irish town. Political rumours, names, appearances, telegrams, seasoned horses at any prices, there could only be one meaning to it. He held a secret and he meant to use it.

Mr. Warner, who was the partner of Mr. Worlington Dodds, and who was suffering from the same eclipse, had gone down to the Stock Exchange, but had found little consolation there, for the European system was in a ferment, and rumours of peace and of a war were succeeding each other with such rapidity and assurance that it was impossible to know which to trust. It was obvious that a fortune lay. either way, for every rumour set the funds fluctuating, but without special information it was impossible to act, and no one dared to plunge heavily upon the strength of news- paper surmise and the gossip of the street Warner knew that an hour's work might resuscitate the fallen fortunes of himself and his partner, and yet he could not afford to make a mistake. He returned to his office in the afternoon, half inclined to back the chances of peace, for of all war scares not one in ten comes to pass. As he entered the office a telegram lay upon the table. It was from Dunsloe, a place of which he had never heard, and was signed by his absent partner. The message was in cypher, but 'he soon translated it, for it was short and crisp. "I am a bear of everything German and French. Sell, sell, sell, keep on selling." For a moment Warner hesitated. What could Worlington Dodds know at Dunsloe which was not known in alfogmorton-street. But he remembered the quickness and decision of his partner. 'de would not have sent such a message without -,cry good grounds. If he was to act at all he 1111 W act at once, so hardening his heart he went down to the house and, dealing upon that curious system by which a man can sell what he had not got and what he could not pay for if he had it, he disposed of heavy parcels of French and German securities. He had caught the market in one of its little spasms of hope, and there was no lack of buying until his . own persistent selling caused others to follow his lead, and so brought about a reaction. When Warner returned to his offices it took him some hours to work out his accounts, and he emerged into the streets in the evening with the absolute certainty that the next settling day would leave him either hopelessly bankrupt or exceedingly prosperous. It all depended upon Worlington Dodds's in- formation. What could he possibly have found out at Dunsloe? _ _

--------- - And then suddenly he saw a newspaper-boy fasten a poster upon a lamp-post, and a little crowd had gathered round it in an instant. One of them waved his hat in the air. Another shouted to a friend across the street. Warner hurried nu
and caught a glimpse of the poster between two craning beads: .
• "Fc.s.xcE Dncar.s WAR 0 N GERmAar.' "By Jove!" cried Warner. "Old Duddfi ir!O right after all." '

WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. An interim meeting of this Board was held in the Board Room at the Workhouse, Warrington, on Wednes- day morning. Mr A J Jolley presided and there were also present Mrs Clay, Messrs T H Ashcroft, A Brooks, William Houghton, A Jolley, Dr Murray, W Mather, G Pilling,J Payton,with J C Sutton(clerk),S Sutton(assist- ant clerk) C H Ward (master) and A Wright (superin- tendent of Padgate Schools.) THE DUTIES OF PUBLIC VACCINATOR. The CLERK reporced that by reason of the decease ef Dr J H Goma!l it was necessary (wider the Consolidated Orders of the Local Government Board to instruct the public vaccinator of an adjoining district to undertake the duties until the appointment of a successor to Dr Gornall. After a brief discussion it was decided to authorize Dr Sephton to continue the late Dr Gornall's duties until such appointment, payment to be made at the rate Specified in the late Dr Gornall's vaccination contract with the Guardians. AN INMATE'S COMPLAINT. The CLERK laid before the Board a letter from the Local Government Board containing a copy of a letter sent by James Keefe, an inmate of the Workhouse making certain complaints as to his treatment and dietary, The Local Government Board requested to be furnished with the Observations of the Guardians thereon The matter was referred to the House Committee. THE DETENTION OF LUNATICS. I circular letter was read from the Local Government Board on the detention of lunatics in Workhouses and upon the state of the law thereon. This communication was also referred to the House Committee for consideration and itwas ordered that the Committee be authorised to obtain additional printed copies for distribution amongst the Guardians and the various officers concerned. THE APPOINTMENTS OF PROBATIONERS. The Local Government Board wrote sanctioning the appointment of A McHugh as probationary nurse upon terms fixed by pe Guardians. A further letter from the Local Government Board sanctioning the appointment of Josephine McEwan as probationary nurse upon simi- lar terms, and also conveying queries with respect to Miss Ryder's appointment and resignation. The clerk was instructed to reply. .• WITHOUT ENCUMBRANCE." A communication was read from the Poor Law Officers' Association advocating the exclusion from advertisements for union officials of the words " with- out encumbrance." It was explained that the Warrington Union when advertising for officials made no such stipulation. This communication was also referred to the Hoarse Com- mittee. IHE THEFTS OF COPPER AT WIDNES, At the Liverpool Assizes on Wednesday, Joseph Tarleton (27), labourer, John Garkwin (30). labourer. Owen M'Conville (22), and John M'Conville (20) marine- store dealers,all of Widnes,were brought up for sentence. Tarleton had been found guilty on Saturday of stealing copper at Widnes, whilst on the same day Gatkwin pleaded guilty to stealing a quantity of the same metal. On Tuesday the two M'Convilles were found guilty of having feloniously , received a bar of copper stolen by the prisoner Garkwin. Prisoners were brought up for sentence on Wednesday The judge sent Tarleton and Garkwin to goal for six calendar months, their conduct, said his lordship was not nearly so bad as that of the men who had encour- aged them by purchasing the metals they had stolen. He did not believe the denials which the two M'Con- villes had had the impudence to make in the box on the previous day. He was convinced they knew that the metal had been stolen, and the roost lenient penalty he could impose would be, nine calendar months' imprison- ment. A Novel Competition—Record Time for Meat "Dressing." Butchers from Liverpool, Warrington, Leeds, Halifax and Sheffield assembled on the Salford Football Ground on Monday night to witness a meat dressing contest between Paul Titzell, Birken- head, champion beef dresser of the world, and J Marsh, Champion sheep dresser, of Manchester. Titzell had to dress a bullock in less time than Marsh dressed a sheep for £5O. Over 2,000 paid high admission fees, while thousands viewed the match from the embankment. Marsh accomplished his task in 3 minutes 524 s..conds, while Titzell occupied but 3 minutes 161 seconds. Councillor Hornby was judge, and A Mills, Birkenhead, time- keeper.

WARRINGTON. Militia Return from Camp. About nine o'clock on Saturday morning the sth Battalion South Lancashire Militia arrived at Bank Quay Station from Aldershot,where they have been in camp for the annual training. The battalion is a strong one. The men were exceedingly bronzed, and appPared to have derived considerable beneit ' from their encampment. They proceedei to Orford Barracks, where they were dismissed. Death of Mrs H. R. Dodd The death occurred at her residence at Burbage, near Buxton on Monday of Mrs 11 R Dodd, wife o f the Rev Canon Dodd (formerly vicar of Stretton). The deceased, who was 60 years of age, was greatly respected by a large cirlle of friends and much sympathy will be felt for the family in the sad bereavement they have sustained. The deceased had been ailing for two years and though the cause of death was a painful internal complaint she passed peacefully away on the day named. ghe was the eldest daughter of the late Dr di eorge Booth Perry, of Melksham, Wiltshire. The remains of the deceased (who leaves six children) will be interred at the Baihage churchyard on Friday next at four o'clock in the afternoon.
